questions.title: GROUPING SETS vs. Separate GROUP BY Queries
questions.prompt: You need a sales report that shows totals by Region, by Product, by Region+Product, and a single grand total, all in one result set. Explain how GROUPING SETS accomplishes this in one query, and how it differs from ROLLUP and CUBE.
questions.modelAnswer: GROUPING SETS lets you specify exactly which combinations of grouping columns you want in a single query, rather than running one GROUP BY per combination and UNION-ing the results. Each set inside the GROUPING SETS list produces its own set of rows: (Region, Product) gives the detail rows, (Region) gives region subtotals, (Product) gives product subtotals, and () gives the grand total. ROLLUP is a shortcut for a specific hierarchy of subtotals -- ROLLUP(Region, Product) automatically generates (Region, Product), (Region), and (), assuming Product rolls up into Region. CUBE goes further and generates every possible combination of the listed columns, including (Product) alone, which ROLLUP does not produce unless you ask for it explicitly. So GROUPING SETS is the general-purpose tool, and ROLLUP/CUBE are convenient shorthand for the two most common patterns -- a single hierarchy and a full cross-tab of subtotals, respectively. GROUPING() or GROUPING_ID() is typically paired with any of these to tell a NULL in a grouping column apart from a NULL that represents 'this is a subtotal row.'
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for GROUPING SETS here because the request is specifically 'these four particular combinations,' not a full cross-tab and not a strict hierarchy. GROUPING SETS((Region, Product), (Region), (Product), ()) gives me exactly the detail rows, region subtotals, product subtotals, and grand total in one query and one scan, instead of writing four separate GROUP BY queries and UNION ALL-ing them together, which also means the optimizer only has to read the base table once. I'd contrast that with ROLLUP, which I'd use if the ask were a single hierarchy like Region then Product -- it's really just a shorthand for a subset of grouping sets following that hierarchy. CUBE I'd reach for only if someone genuinely wanted every possible combination, including a Product-only subtotal with no Region breakdown, since CUBE on two columns generates four grouping levels, not three. The detail that trips people up across all three is distinguishing an actual NULL value in the data from a NULL that SQL Server inserted to mark a subtotal row -- that's exactly what GROUPING() is for, and I always include it when a report needs to visually label subtotal rows.
questions.example:
SELECT Region, Product, SUM(SalesAmount) AS Total,
       GROUPING(Region) AS IsRegionSubtotal, GROUPING(Product) AS IsProductSubtotal
FROM Sales
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((Region, Product), (Region), (Product), ());
commonMistakes: Writing four separate GROUP BY queries and UNION-ing them when GROUPING SETS does it in one pass
Assuming CUBE and ROLLUP on the same two columns produce the same number of grouping levels
Not using GROUPING() to distinguish a real NULL value from a subtotal-row NULL
Forgetting ROLLUP respects column order as a hierarchy, so ROLLUP(Product, Region) rolls up differently than ROLLUP(Region, Product)
keyPoints: GROUPING SETS lets you specify exact grouping combinations in one query
ROLLUP is a shorthand for a single hierarchical set of subtotals
CUBE generates every possible combination of the listed columns
GROUPING()/GROUPING_ID() disambiguates real NULLs from subtotal-row NULLs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what GROUPING SETS produces
Correctly distinguishes ROLLUP's hierarchical shorthand
Correctly distinguishes CUBE's full combination behavior
Mentions GROUPING() for subtotal-row identification

questions.title: Scalar UDFs vs. Inline Table-Valued Functions
questions.prompt: A colleague wrote a scalar UDF that calculates a customer's lifetime discount tier and calls it in the SELECT list of a query touching a million-row customer table. The query is slow. Explain why, and what you'd change.
questions.modelAnswer: A scalar UDF, in older SQL Server compatibility levels and even in many real-world cases on newer ones, defeats batch-mode execution -- the engine effectively has to call the function once per row, row by row, which turns what should be a set-based operation into a disguised cursor. On a million-row table that per-row function-call overhead adds up fast, and worse, a scalar UDF referenced in a WHERE clause also makes that predicate non-SARGable, so any index on the filtered column can't be used efficiently either. The fix is to rewrite the logic as an inline table-valued function (iTVF) instead of a scalar UDF. An iTVF is just a parameterized view under the hood -- SQL Server expands its single RETURN (SELECT ...) statement directly into the calling query's plan and optimizes it as one set-based statement, so you get the reusable logic without the row-by-row penalty. If the logic is simple enough, inlining it directly as a CASE expression or a computed column in the query itself is even better, since it avoids any function-call indirection at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I've hit this exact problem before, and the first thing I'd check is whether it's a scalar function being called in the SELECT list of a large query -- that's almost always the culprit. Scalar UDFs force row-by-row evaluation; SQL Server can't fold the function's logic into the surrounding set-based plan, so a million rows means a million individual function invocations, and that overhead is brutal compared to a native expression. My fix is almost always to convert it into an inline table-valued function, because an iTVF is really just a single SELECT statement that SQL Server can inline and optimize as part of the outer query -- same reusable logic, but it behaves like a view instead of a cursor in disguise. If the discount-tier logic is genuinely simple -- a few CASE WHEN thresholds -- I'd go even further and just write it directly as a CASE expression in the query, skip the function call entirely, and save the abstraction for logic that's actually complex enough to need it.
commonMistakes: Assuming any UDF is equally bad for performance, without distinguishing scalar UDFs from inline TVFs
Not realizing a scalar UDF in a WHERE clause makes the predicate non-SARGable
Reaching for a multi-statement TVF when an inline TVF would optimize far better
Not profiling to confirm the UDF is actually the bottleneck before rewriting it
keyPoints: Scalar UDFs typically force row-by-row evaluation on large result sets
A scalar UDF in a WHERE clause makes that predicate non-SARGable
Inline table-valued functions get inlined into the calling query's plan and optimized as a set
Simple logic is often better inlined directly as a CASE expression

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses row-by-row scalar UDF execution as the cause
Recommends converting to an inline table-valued function
Mentions the SARGability impact or the CASE-expression alternative

questions.title: AFTER Triggers vs. INSTEAD OF Triggers
questions.prompt: Explain the difference between an AFTER trigger and an INSTEAD OF trigger in SQL Server, and describe a realistic scenario where you'd need an INSTEAD OF trigger specifically.
questions.modelAnswer: An AFTER trigger fires once the triggering INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE has already been applied to the table -- the rows exist in their new form, and the trigger runs as a follow-up action, commonly used for auditing, cascading business logic, or enforcing cross-table rules that a constraint can't express. An INSTEAD OF trigger fires in place of the triggering statement -- the base action never actually happens unless the trigger's own code performs it. This matters most on views: a view built from a join across multiple base tables generally isn't directly updatable by SQL Server's rules, so an INSTEAD OF trigger on that view lets you intercept the INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statement and manually write the logic that updates each underlying table correctly. A realistic case: a 'CustomerSummary' view joining Customer and Address: without an INSTEAD OF trigger, an UPDATE against that view would fail outright; with one, you can parse the attempted change and route the Customer columns to the Customer table and the Address columns to the Address table.
questions.professionalAnswer: The core distinction I'd give is timing and whether the original action actually happens on its own. AFTER triggers run once the data's already changed -- so by the time my trigger code runs, the INSERT or UPDATE is already committed to the table, which is why AFTER triggers are my default for things like writing an audit row or enforcing a rule that spans multiple tables. INSTEAD OF triggers are different -- they completely replace the triggering statement, so nothing happens to the base table unless I write code inside the trigger that makes it happen. The place I've actually needed this is on a multi-table view -- say a view joining Customer and Address so reporting tools get one flat row per customer. SQL Server won't let you UPDATE that view directly because it can't figure out which base table each column belongs to, so I'd put an INSTEAD OF UPDATE trigger on the view that inspects which columns changed and issues the correct UPDATE against Customer and against Address separately.
commonMistakes: Thinking an INSTEAD OF trigger runs in addition to the base action rather than replacing it entirely
Using an AFTER trigger on a non-updatable multi-table view and being surprised the base UPDATE still fails
Forgetting both trigger types rely on the inserted/deleted pseudo-tables to see what changed
Writing business logic in a trigger that would be clearer and more maintainable as a stored procedure
keyPoints: AFTER triggers fire once the change has already been applied to the base table
INSTEAD OF triggers replace the triggering statement entirely
INSTEAD OF triggers are the standard way to make a non-updatable view accept DML
Both rely on the inserted/deleted pseudo-tables to inspect the attempted change

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains AFTER trigger timing
Correctly explains INSTEAD OF trigger replacement behavior
Gives a realistic, correct scenario needing INSTEAD OF

questions.title: Read Committed Snapshot vs. Serializable Isolation
questions.prompt: A reporting query is being blocked by a long-running OLTP transaction on the same table. Explain how enabling Read Committed Snapshot Isolation (RCSI) would change that, and why you would almost never reach for SERIALIZABLE to solve the same problem.
questions.modelAnswer: Under the default READ COMMITTED isolation level, a reader has to wait for a writer's locks to release before it can read a row, which is exactly why a long-running OLTP transaction blocks a reporting query. RCSI changes what READ COMMITTED means at the database level: instead of taking shared locks and waiting, readers are given a transactionally consistent snapshot of the row as it existed at the start of the statement, using row versions stored in tempdb's version store. The reporting query no longer blocks on the writer's locks -- it just reads the last-committed version of the row instead of waiting for the in-flight transaction to finish. SERIALIZABLE goes in the opposite direction entirely: it's the strictest isolation level, taking range locks to prevent other transactions from inserting or modifying rows that would affect the current transaction's result set if re-run, which increases blocking and lock contention rather than reducing it. It solves phantom reads and non-repeatable reads, not reader/writer blocking, so reaching for it to fix a blocking reporting query would make the problem worse, not better.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame this as 'RCSI removes the wait, SERIALIZABLE adds more of it.' The blocking happens because under plain READ COMMITTED, my reporting query needs a shared lock, and it can't get one while the OLTP transaction is holding an exclusive lock on the same rows -- so it just sits there waiting. Turning on RCSI at the database level changes the behavior of READ COMMITTED itself: now my reporting query gets a row-versioned snapshot of the data as of the start of its statement, pulled from tempdb's version store, instead of fighting for a lock. It doesn't block, and it doesn't see uncommitted data either -- it's a real, consistent point-in-time view. SERIALIZABLE would be the wrong direction completely -- it's the most locking-heavy isolation level SQL Server has, designed to prevent phantom rows by locking ranges, and using it here would make my reporting query more likely to block others and get blocked itself, not less. The one tradeoff I'd flag with RCSI is the extra tempdb load from maintaining those row versions, which is worth monitoring on a busy OLTP system before turning it on.
questions.example:
ALTER DATABASE SalesDB SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON;
-- Reporting queries under READ COMMITTED now read a versioned snapshot instead of blocking on the OLTP transaction's locks.
commonMistakes: Confusing RCSI with SNAPSHOT isolation, which requires an explicit SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL per session
Reaching for NOLOCK as the fix instead of RCSI, introducing dirty reads unnecessarily
Assuming SERIALIZABLE reduces blocking rather than increasing it
Forgetting RCSI adds tempdb version-store overhead that needs monitoring on write-heavy systems
keyPoints: Default READ COMMITTED makes readers wait for writer locks to release
RCSI gives readers a row-versioned snapshot instead, eliminating that wait
RCSI is a database-level setting, distinct from session-level SNAPSHOT isolation
SERIALIZABLE increases locking and blocking; it solves phantom reads, not reader/writer contention
RCSI's tradeoff is additional load on tempdb's version store

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why default READ COMMITTED blocks here
Correctly explains RCSI's row-versioning mechanism
Correctly explains why SERIALIZABLE would not help
Mentions a real tradeoff of enabling RCSI

questions.title: Window Frame: RANGE vs. ROWS
questions.prompt: You're computing a running total with SUM(...) OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate). Explain the default frame this uses, why two orders placed on the same date can produce a surprising result, and how switching to ROWS fixes it.
questions.modelAnswer: When you write ORDER BY inside an OVER() clause without an explicit frame, SQL Server defaults to RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. RANGE operates on logical peer groups defined by the ORDER BY value, not on physical row position -- so every row that shares the same ORDER BY value as the current row is treated as part of the 'current row' for frame purposes. If two orders share the exact same OrderDate, RANGE's default frame includes both of them as peers, and both rows get the same running total -- the combined total through that date -- rather than one getting the total through the first order and the other getting the total through the second. Switching to ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW changes the frame to be based on physical row position instead of logical value peers, so each row gets its own distinct running total based on its position in the ordered sequence, breaking the tie using whatever order the engine processes rows in (which should be made deterministic with a tiebreaker column in the ORDER BY, like OrderID).
questions.professionalAnswer: This is one of those defaults that looks fine until you hit same-day duplicates, so I always call it out explicitly. If I just write SUM(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate), SQL Server quietly defaults to RANGE, and RANGE thinks in terms of value peer groups, not row position -- any rows tied on OrderDate are treated as the same logical point, so they all get the same cumulative total, which reads as a bug to anyone checking the numbers row by row. The fix is to be explicit and switch to ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which frames by physical row position instead, so each row in a tie gets its own distinct running total based on where it lands in the sort order. But switching to ROWS alone isn't quite enough on its own -- if OrderDate still has ties, the 'where it lands' part is ambiguous unless I add a tiebreaker to the ORDER BY, like OrderID, so the running total is fully deterministic and reproducible every time the query runs.
questions.example:
-- Default RANGE: same-date orders get the SAME running total
SUM(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate)

-- Fixed with ROWS and a tiebreaker: each order gets its own running total
SUM(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY OrderDate, OrderID ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
commonMistakes: Not knowing RANGE is the silent default when no frame is specified
Assuming RANGE and ROWS always produce identical results, missing the tie-handling difference
Switching to ROWS but forgetting to add a tiebreaker column, leaving the result order-dependent
Using RANGE with a non-integer or non-date frame extent, which SQL Server doesn't fully support anyway
keyPoints: RANGE is the default frame and operates on logical value peer groups
ROWS operates on physical row position regardless of value ties
Tied ORDER BY values under RANGE all receive the same aggregated result
A tiebreaker column in ORDER BY is needed alongside ROWS for a fully deterministic result

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies RANGE as the silent default
Correctly explains the peer-group tie behavior under RANGE
Correctly explains how ROWS changes the behavior
Mentions the need for a deterministic tiebreaker

questions.title: QUALIFY: Snowflake's Shortcut for Filtering Window Functions
questions.prompt: In Snowflake you can write WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1 using QUALIFY instead. Explain what QUALIFY does, why T-SQL has no equivalent keyword, and how you'd write the same logic in T-SQL.
questions.modelAnswer: QUALIFY is a Snowflake (and BigQuery) clause that filters rows based on the result of a window function, applied logically after the window function is computed but in a single, flat statement -- no subquery or CTE required. It exists because window functions can't be referenced directly in a WHERE clause: WHERE is evaluated before window functions are computed in the logical query processing order, so SQL Server has no keyword that lets you filter on a window function result in the same SELECT. T-SQL's standard workaround is to compute the window function in a CTE or subquery, then filter on it in the outer WHERE clause once it's a regular column. The two approaches are logically equivalent -- QUALIFY is pure syntactic convenience, not a different capability -- but the T-SQL version requires wrapping the logic in an extra layer because T-SQL has no way to filter on a window function result at the same query level it's computed in.
questions.professionalAnswer: QUALIFY is honestly just a convenience keyword, and I'd explain it that way rather than making it sound more exotic than it is. It lets you write a filter directly against a window function's result -- most commonly ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1 for deduplication -- without needing a wrapping CTE. T-SQL doesn't have it because of how logical query processing order works: WHERE is evaluated before window functions get computed, so by the time WHERE would run, ROW_NUMBER() hasn't been evaluated yet in that same SELECT. Snowflake's QUALIFY is a separate logical step that runs after window functions are computed, which is exactly the gap T-SQL doesn't fill with a keyword. In T-SQL I'd get the same result with a CTE: compute ROW_NUMBER() inside the CTE, then filter WHERE RowNum = 1 in the outer query referencing the CTE. Functionally identical, just one extra layer of nesting -- when I move between dialects I don't think of this as 'T-SQL is missing a feature,' just a different place in the query where the same filter has to live.
commonMistakes: Trying to write WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1 directly in T-SQL and being surprised it fails
Thinking QUALIFY does something a CTE-based filter can't logically achieve
Not knowing which dialects support QUALIFY (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks SQL) versus which don't (T-SQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle)
Forgetting QUALIFY still requires the window function to be present in the SELECT or available to reference
keyPoints: QUALIFY filters on a window function result in the same flat SELECT statement
WHERE is evaluated before window functions in logical query processing order, which is why it can't do this
T-SQL achieves the same result with a CTE or subquery wrapping the window function
QUALIFY is syntactic convenience, not a different logical capability

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what QUALIFY does
Correctly explains why WHERE can't filter on a window function directly
Provides a correct T-SQL equivalent

questions.title: Pagination Across SQL Dialects
questions.prompt: You need to return rows 21-30 of a result set. Show how you'd do this in T-SQL, in a dialect that supports LIMIT/OFFSET (Snowflake/PostgreSQL/MySQL), and briefly describe how older Oracle syntax (ROWNUM) handles the same problem. Why does ORDER BY matter more here than people expect?
questions.modelAnswer: T-SQL uses OFFSET ... FETCH NEXT ... ROWS ONLY, which requires an ORDER BY clause to be present since the whole concept of 'skip 20, take 10' is only meaningful against an ordered sequence. Dialects like Snowflake, PostgreSQL, and MySQL use the more compact LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20, which is functionally equivalent but with the two numbers in the opposite order visually (rows-to-return first, skip-count second) compared to T-SQL. Older Oracle syntax (pre-12c) has no LIMIT/OFFSET at all and instead relies on the pseudo-column ROWNUM, which is assigned to rows as they're returned by the query -- which means you have to wrap the ordered query in a subquery first, because ROWNUM is assigned before ORDER BY is applied in the outer query, then filter ROWNUM in an outer WHERE clause (commonly ROWNUM BETWEEN 21 AND 30 against a pre-ordered subquery). The ORDER BY matters more than people expect because without a guaranteed, fully deterministic order, 'rows 21-30' is not a stable concept at all -- the database is free to return rows in any physical order it finds convenient, so the exact same query can return different rows 21-30 on different executions unless the ORDER BY columns are unique enough to break every tie.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd show all three because I've worked across more than one of these stacks. In T-SQL it's ORDER BY ... OFFSET 20 ROWS FETCH NEXT 10 ROWS ONLY, and SQL Server actually requires the ORDER BY to be present for this syntax to even parse. In Snowflake or Postgres it's LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20 -- same idea, just flipped order of the two numbers, which trips people up moving between stacks more than it should. Oracle's classic ROWNUM approach is the one that actually requires care: ROWNUM gets assigned to rows as the database produces them, before any ORDER BY in that same query takes effect, so if I want 'rows 21 through 30 by some sort order,' I have to put the ORDER BY inside a subquery first, then apply ROWNUM filtering in the outer query against the now-ordered result. But honestly, the detail I care about most in all three dialects is the same: pagination is only meaningful with a fully deterministic ORDER BY. If I'm ordering by something with ties -- like OrderDate alone -- 'page 3' isn't guaranteed to be the same set of rows every time I run the query, so I always add a unique tiebreaker column to the ORDER BY before I trust pagination in production.
commonMistakes: Forgetting T-SQL's OFFSET/FETCH syntax requires an ORDER BY clause to be present
Flipping the LIMIT/OFFSET argument order between dialects out of habit
Applying ROWNUM filtering before the inner ORDER BY is applied, instead of in a wrapping outer query
Paginating on a non-unique ORDER BY and getting inconsistent pages across runs
keyPoints: T-SQL uses OFFSET/FETCH and requires ORDER BY to be present
LIMIT/OFFSET dialects reverse the visual order of the two numbers compared to T-SQL
Classic Oracle ROWNUM must be filtered in an outer query after an inner ORDER BY
Deterministic pagination requires a unique tiebreaker in the ORDER BY

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly writes T-SQL OFFSET/FETCH syntax
Correctly writes LIMIT/OFFSET syntax
Correctly explains the ROWNUM subquery pattern
Explains why a deterministic ORDER BY is required for stable pagination

questions.title: Query Folding in Power Query
questions.prompt: Explain what query folding is in Power Query, why a step like a Table.AddColumn with a complex custom M function often breaks it, and how you'd confirm whether folding is still happening at a given step.
questions.modelAnswer: Query folding is Power Query's ability to translate the steps you apply in the Power Query editor -- filters, column selections, merges, aggregations -- back into native query language (SQL, for a relational source) and push that work down to the source system, instead of pulling the raw data into Power BI's engine and transforming it locally. This matters enormously for performance: folding a filter back to the source means only the rows you actually need cross the network, while an unfolded step means the entire source table gets pulled first and the transformation happens row by row inside Power Query's own engine, which is far slower for anything beyond a small table. A custom M function, especially one with row-by-row logic inside Table.AddColumn, typically can't be translated into the source's native query language at all -- there's often no SQL equivalent for an arbitrary M expression -- so the moment that step runs, folding stops there and every subsequent step operates on data already pulled into memory, even if those later steps would have been foldable on their own. You confirm whether folding is still active by right-clicking a step in the Query Dependencies/Applied Steps pane and checking whether 'View Native Query' is available and enabled; once it's greyed out, that step (or an earlier one) broke the chain.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of query folding as Power Query trying to rewrite my clicks as a native query the source database can run itself, instead of doing the work locally. When it works, a filter I apply becomes part of the WHERE clause sent to SQL Server, and only the filtered rows ever leave the source. The problem with a complex custom M function inside something like Table.AddColumn is that there's often no way to express that logic as SQL at all -- it might be calling other M functions, doing conditional logic Power Query's folding engine doesn't know how to translate -- so the moment that step executes, Power Query just gives up on folding from there forward, even if the step after it would have folded fine on its own. In practice this means step order matters: I try to put every foldable operation -- filters, column selection, simple merges -- before any custom column logic, so the heavy lifting happens at the source, not locally in Power Query. To check it, I right-click each step in Applied Steps and look at whether 'View Native Query' is available; the step right before it stops being clickable is exactly where folding broke.
questions.example: A query that filters rows then adds a custom M column, versus one that adds the custom column first then filters: in the first version, the filter folds to the source and only matching rows transfer; in the second, every row transfers first because the custom column step already broke folding before the filter ever ran.
commonMistakes: Adding custom M logic early in the query, breaking folding for every step that follows
Assuming folding always happens regardless of source type, when it depends on the connector supporting translation
Not checking 'View Native Query' to confirm folding status before assuming performance problems are elsewhere
Blending data from two different source types and expecting the whole combined query to fold
keyPoints: Query folding pushes Power Query steps down to the source as native queries
Folding drastically reduces data transferred and processing time versus local transformation
A custom M function often can't be translated to the source's native query language
Once folding breaks at a step, no later step in that query folds either
'View Native Query' on a step confirms whether folding is still active

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what query folding is and why it matters
Correctly explains why custom M logic breaks folding
Correctly describes how to verify folding status

questions.title: ALL vs. ALLSELECTED vs. ALLEXCEPT
questions.prompt: A '% of Total' measure uses CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), ALL(Sales)) as its denominator, but it shows the wrong percentage whenever a user applies a slicer. Explain why, and which function fixes it.
questions.code:
Pct of Total =
DIVIDE(
    SUM(Sales[Amount]),
    CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), ALL(Sales))
)
questions.modelAnswer: ALL(Sales) removes every filter on the Sales table entirely -- including any filter coming from a slicer on the report page -- so the denominator always equals the grand total across the whole unfiltered table, regardless of what the user has selected. That's the wrong behavior for a '% of a filtered subset' measure: if a user slices to Region = 'West', they almost certainly want each row's percentage of the West total, not of the entire company's total, and ALL ignores that intent completely. ALLSELECTED(Sales) is the fix for exactly this case -- it removes filters coming from inside the current visual's own row/column context, but preserves filters coming from outside the visual, such as slicers and report-level filters, which is what lets the denominator respect the user's selection while still removing the per-row filter context needed to get back to a total. ALLEXCEPT is a different tool for a different problem -- it removes all filters on a table except the ones you explicitly name, useful when you want a total within one dimension (like a region subtotal) while ignoring filters on every other column of that same table.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a really common gotcha, and it comes down to ALL not caring at all about what the user clicked. ALL(Sales) wipes every filter off the table, full stop -- no matter what slicer is active, the denominator is always the grand total for the entire dataset. That's not what '% of total' usually means to a business user, though -- if they've sliced to one region, they expect each row to show its percent of that region's total, not the whole company's. ALLSELECTED is the function built for exactly this situation: it strips out the filter context that comes from the visual itself -- the row and column headers in the matrix, for instance -- but it keeps whatever's been selected outside the visual, like a slicer or a report-level filter. So with ALLSELECTED, if the user slices to West, my denominator becomes the West total, and the percentages inside the visual are relative to what they're actually looking at. I'd save ALLEXCEPT for a different need entirely -- when I want to clear filters on every column of a table except one or two I deliberately keep, which is a 'subtotal by this one dimension' pattern, not a 'respect what the user picked' pattern.
questions.example:
Pct of Total (Respects Slicer) =
DIVIDE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), ALLSELECTED(Sales)))
-- With a Region slicer set to West, this now divides by the West total, not the grand total.
commonMistakes: Using ALL when the intent is actually 'respect external filters, ignore the visual's own context'
Assuming ALLSELECTED removes every filter the way ALL does
Confusing ALLEXCEPT's 'keep these columns filtered, clear everything else' behavior with ALLSELECTED's visual-vs-external distinction
Not testing the measure with an actual slicer applied before shipping it
keyPoints: ALL removes every filter on a table, including slicers and report-level filters
ALLSELECTED removes the visual's own filter context but preserves external filters like slicers
ALLEXCEPT clears all filters on a table except the explicitly named columns
Choosing the wrong one is a common source of '% of total' measures that ignore user selections

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses why ALL ignores the slicer
Correctly identifies ALLSELECTED as the fix and explains its behavior
Correctly distinguishes ALLEXCEPT's different use case

questions.title: LOD Expressions and Filter Order of Operations
questions.prompt: A Tableau dashboard uses a FIXED LOD expression to compute each customer's first purchase date, then a dashboard filter is applied to show only orders from this year. The FIXED calculation's result doesn't change when the filter is applied, which confuses a stakeholder. Explain why, and how you'd change it if they actually wanted the filter to affect the LOD result.
questions.modelAnswer: Tableau's filters execute in a specific order, and where a LOD expression's filter dependency falls in that order determines whether a given filter affects it. Dimension filters, by default, are categorized as either 'Context Filters' (which run early, before LOD expressions are computed) or ordinary filters, which by default for a FIXED LOD run after the FIXED expression's computation, not before it. Because FIXED hard-codes its own grouping dimensions and ignores whatever else is in view, an ordinary filter applied to the view doesn't retroactively change what FIXED computed -- it only filters the rows the already-computed FIXED values are displayed alongside. So 'first purchase date per customer' computed via FIXED gets calculated across all of that customer's orders regardless of the year filter, and the year filter only controls which rows show up in the view afterward -- it doesn't make the FIXED calculation recompute using only this year's orders. If the actual intent is for the filter to be applied before the LOD computation, the fix is to add the filter as a Context Filter, which forces it to run before FIXED calculations are computed, so FIXED then only sees the already-filtered subset of rows.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk the stakeholder through Tableau's order of operations, because this is one of the most common 'why isn't my filter working' moments with LOD expressions. By default, a regular filter you drag onto the Filters shelf runs after FIXED expressions are computed -- so FIXED Customer : MIN(Order Date) calculates each customer's true first purchase date across their entire order history first, and only afterward does the year filter decide which rows get displayed. That's exactly why the stakeholder sees the same first-purchase date whether or not the filter is applied -- the filter never touched the calculation itself. If what they actually want is 'first purchase date within this year only,' I have two options: either change the filter to a Context Filter, which moves it earlier in the order of operations so FIXED only ever sees the filtered rows, or switch the LOD type to INCLUDE, which does respect view-level filters differently than FIXED does, depending on exactly what dimension it needs to add. I'd usually reach for the Context Filter fix first, because it's the more explicit, commonly-understood lever for this exact problem.
questions.example:
FIXED Expr: { FIXED [Customer] : MIN([Order Date]) } -- always computed across ALL of a customer's orders.
Making the Year filter a Context Filter forces it to run before this FIXED expression, so only orders from the selected year are ever visible to the calculation.
commonMistakes: Assuming any dashboard filter automatically affects every LOD expression's result
Not knowing the difference between Context Filters and ordinary filters in Tableau's order of operations
Reaching for INCLUDE/EXCLUDE without understanding why FIXED specifically ignores view-level filters
Changing a filter to a Context Filter without warning the team it can also change performance characteristics

Context Filters run earlier in Tableau's order of operations, before FIXED calculations
Making a filter a Context Filter is the standard fix when a FIXED result needs to respect it

Correctly identifies Context Filters as the standard fix

questions.title: Azure Data Factory CI/CD: Git, ARM Templates, and adf_publish
questions.prompt: Explain how Git integration changes the way an ADF pipeline moves from development to production, what the adf_publish branch actually contains, and why 'just publish from the UI' is not a safe production deployment process on a team.
questions.modelAnswer: Without Git integration, an ADF factory's resources live only in the live service, edited directly through the portal, with no change history and no way to review or roll back a change before it goes live. Connecting the factory to a Git repository changes this fundamentally: every pipeline, dataset, and linked service definition becomes a JSON file tracked in a feature-branch workflow, so changes go through pull requests, code review, and a real commit history, just like application code. Clicking 'Publish' in the ADF UI doesn't deploy to production directly either -- it takes the current state of your collaboration branch (commonly main or master) and generates ARM templates representing the whole factory's resources, committing them to a separate adf_publish branch that Git integration creates automatically. That adf_publish branch is the actual deployable artifact -- an Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions release pipeline picks up those ARM templates and deploys them to the test or production ADF instance using an ARM template deployment task, typically with environment-specific parameters swapped in for things like linked service connection strings. Publishing straight from the UI without this pipeline is unsafe on a team because it bypasses code review, there's no approval gate before a change reaches production, and there's no consistent way to promote the exact same, tested set of changes through dev, test, and prod environments in sequence.
questions.professionalAnswer: The way I'd frame it: without Git, ADF is basically a live editor with no undo history visible to the team -- every change happens directly against the service. Connecting a Git repo turns pipelines, datasets, and linked services into actual files, so changes go through branches and pull requests like any other code, which means someone reviews a change before it merges to the main collaboration branch. Clicking Publish doesn't push straight to production, though -- what it actually does is take the main branch's current state and generate ARM templates representing the entire factory, which get committed to the adf_publish branch that ADF's Git integration manages automatically. That branch is what a release pipeline in Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions actually deploys from, parameterizing things like connection strings so the same ARM templates can be deployed to dev, test, and prod with different settings each time. Publishing straight from the portal UI with no pipeline behind it skips all of that -- no review, no approval gate, no guarantee that what's in test is actually what gets promoted to prod, which is exactly the kind of gap that causes a surprise production outage nobody can trace back to a specific reviewed change.
questions.example: Git-connected ADF factory: feature branch -> PR -> merge to main -> Publish generates ARM templates on adf_publish -> Azure DevOps release pipeline deploys those templates to Test, then (after approval) to Prod, substituting environment-specific linked service parameters each time.
commonMistakes: Assuming Publish in the ADF UI deploys directly to a separate production factory
Not realizing adf_publish is an auto-managed branch containing generated ARM templates, not hand-edited JSON
Skipping a release pipeline and manually importing ARM templates into production ad hoc
Hardcoding environment-specific values into pipeline JSON instead of parameterizing them for ARM template deployment
keyPoints: Git integration turns ADF resources into reviewable, version-controlled JSON files
Publish generates ARM templates from the collaboration branch and commits them to adf_publish
A release pipeline deploys those ARM templates to each environment with parameterized settings
Publishing directly from the UI bypasses review, approval gates, and consistent environment promotion

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what Git integration changes about the development workflow
Correctly explains what Publish and the adf_publish branch actually contain
Correctly explains the risk of publishing directly from the UI on a team

questions.title: Snowflake Time Travel vs. Fail-safe
questions.prompt: A teammate accidentally dropped and recreated a Snowflake table two days ago, and separately a table was truncated 10 days ago. Explain what recovery options exist for each situation, and why one of them might require contacting Snowflake support.
questions.modelAnswer: Time Travel lets you query, clone, or restore a table's data as it existed at a past point in time within a configurable retention window -- up to 1 day on Standard edition, up to 90 days on Enterprise edition and above, set per table or database via DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS. For the table dropped and recreated two days ago, as long as that's within the retention window, UNDROP TABLE can restore the dropped table directly (provided the name isn't already taken by the newly recreated table, in which case you'd rename one first), or you could query the table's historical state with AT/BEFORE syntax and a specific timestamp before it was dropped. Fail-safe is a separate, non-configurable 7-day period that begins only after Time Travel's retention window ends, and it exists purely as a last-resort disaster recovery mechanism -- customers cannot query or restore Fail-safe data themselves at all; only Snowflake support can perform that recovery, and typically only for a genuine data loss event, not routine 'oops' recovery. The table truncated 10 days ago is the harder case: if Time Travel retention was only the default 1 day, that window closed long ago, and depending on the exact retention setting, the data might now be in the Fail-safe period (requiring a Snowflake support ticket) or already gone entirely if even Fail-safe's 7 days have elapsed since retention ended.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd handle these as two different levels of urgency. The table dropped and recreated two days ago is the easy one, assuming a reasonable retention window is configured -- Snowflake's Time Travel keeps a recoverable history of a table's past states, and UNDROP TABLE is literally built for exactly this accident. If the name's already taken by the new table, I'd just rename the new one out of the way first, undrop the old one, then reconcile. The truncated table from 10 days ago worries me more, because Time Travel retention defaults to 1 day unless someone explicitly raised DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS, so that window's probably already closed. At that point we're relying on Fail-safe, which is a 7-day period that kicks in automatically after Time Travel ends -- but critically, nobody on my team can self-serve recover from Fail-safe. That's Snowflake support only, and it's meant as a true last resort, not a convenience feature, so I'd open a support case immediately rather than waiting, because every day that passes closes that window further, and if we're already past both windows combined, that data is genuinely gone.
commonMistakes: Assuming Fail-safe is self-service recovery like Time Travel, rather than Snowflake-support-only
Not checking the table's actual DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS before assuming recovery is possible
Forgetting UNDROP fails if a table with the same name already exists
Confusing Fail-safe's fixed 7-day window with Time Travel's configurable 1-90 day window
keyPoints: Time Travel allows self-service querying, cloning, and restoring within a configurable retention window
UNDROP TABLE restores a dropped table within that retention window
Fail-safe is a fixed, non-configurable 7-day period after Time Travel ends
Fail-safe recovery requires contacting Snowflake support and is intended as a last resort

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains Time Travel and UNDROP for the recent accident
Correctly explains Fail-safe's scope and support-only access
Correctly reasons about the 10-day-old truncation's recovery risk

questions.title: Direct Lake Mode vs. Import and DirectQuery in Fabric
questions.prompt: Explain how Direct Lake mode in Microsoft Fabric differs from both Import mode and DirectQuery mode, and describe one real condition that would cause a Direct Lake semantic model to silently fall back to DirectQuery.
questions.modelAnswer: Import mode loads a full copy of the data into the Power BI dataset's in-memory VertiPaq engine, giving the fastest query performance but requiring a refresh cycle to pick up new data. DirectQuery sends a native query back to the source for every visual interaction, so it's always live but pays a per-query latency cost and loses most VertiPaq-level performance optimizations. Direct Lake mode is a third option specific to Fabric: it reads Delta Lake Parquet files directly from OneLake into VertiPaq's in-memory structures without a traditional ETL-style refresh and without going through a query-generation layer like DirectQuery does -- it's effectively loading the same columnar data Import would use, but reading it straight off the lake's physical files, which gives near-Import performance with much fresher data and no separate copy to maintain. The real condition that causes a silent fallback to DirectQuery is when a query needs something Direct Lake's engine can't currently serve directly from the Delta files -- for example, a visual or measure that triggers a request against columns or row-level security conditions beyond what's been "framed" into memory, or certain complex DAX patterns Direct Lake doesn't fully support yet; Fabric capacity admins can also disable fallback entirely, in which case the query would fail outright instead of silently falling back.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame these three as different tradeoffs between freshness and speed. Import is the fastest because everything's already sitting in VertiPaq's optimized in-memory format, but it's only as fresh as the last scheduled refresh. DirectQuery is always current because it queries the source live, but every click in the report pays a round trip to that source, which can get painfully slow. Direct Lake is Fabric's answer to getting both -- it reads the Delta Parquet files sitting in OneLake directly into VertiPaq's columnar structures, so it behaves almost like Import for performance, but without a separate copy-and-refresh cycle, because it's reading the same files the lakehouse already has. The gotcha I'd flag is that Direct Lake isn't guaranteed to serve every query itself -- if something in a report hits a limitation the engine can't handle directly off the lake files, Fabric will quietly fall back to DirectQuery behind the scenes for that query, and the user won't necessarily notice except that performance drops unexpectedly. I've seen this happen specifically around RLS scenarios and certain DAX patterns that Direct Lake doesn't support yet, and it's worth knowing the fallback can be disabled by a capacity admin, in which case you get an outright error instead of a silent slowdown.
questions.example: A Direct Lake semantic model performing well in testing suddenly gets slower in production once a complex RLS rule referencing a non-framed column is added, because that specific query pattern silently falls back to DirectQuery against the underlying Fabric Lakehouse SQL endpoint.
commonMistakes: Describing Direct Lake as 'just another name for Import' without noting it reads lake files directly, not a separately copied dataset
Assuming Direct Lake always matches Import-level performance with no exceptions
Not knowing fallback to DirectQuery can happen silently for unsupported query patterns
Forgetting a capacity admin can disable fallback, turning unsupported queries into hard errors instead
keyPoints: Import loads a full in-memory copy requiring scheduled refresh
DirectQuery queries the source live for every interaction, trading speed for freshness
Direct Lake reads Delta Parquet files from OneLake directly into VertiPaq structures
Direct Lake can silently fall back to DirectQuery for unsupported query patterns unless fallback is disabled

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly contrasts all three modes
Correctly explains Direct Lake's relationship to OneLake/Delta files
Gives a real, accurate fallback condition

questions.title: Delta Lake's Transaction Log and Schema Evolution
questions.prompt: Explain how Delta Lake's transaction log gives Parquet files on cloud storage ACID guarantees, and the difference between schema enforcement and schema evolution when a new column shows up in incoming data.
questions.modelAnswer: A Delta table is really just a directory of Parquet files plus a transaction log (the _delta_log folder) that records every change made to the table as an ordered sequence of JSON commit files, periodically checkpointed into Parquet for efficiency. Readers and writers agree on the true state of the table by reading this log, not by scanning the raw files directly -- a write operation adds new Parquet files and then atomically commits a new log entry listing exactly which files are now part of the table and which are removed, and that atomic commit (using optimistic concurrency control against cloud object storage) is what gives Delta its ACID guarantees: a reader either sees the complete pre-write state or the complete post-write state, never a half-finished write, because they're only ever reading a specific, fully-committed log version. Schema enforcement is the default behavior: if an incoming write includes a column that doesn't match the table's existing schema, or has the wrong data type, Delta rejects the write outright, which protects a production table from silently absorbing malformed or unexpected data. Schema evolution is the opt-in alternative -- passing mergeSchema=true (or the equivalent setting) tells Delta to accept a new column by adding it to the table's schema going forward, with existing rows getting NULL for that column, rather than rejecting the write; it's deliberately opt-in because allowing it unconditionally would let schema drift creep into a table unnoticed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe the transaction log as the thing that turns 'a folder of Parquet files' into an actual reliable table. Every write to a Delta table doesn't just drop new Parquet files into the directory -- it also appends a new entry to the _delta_log describing exactly what changed, and that log entry is written atomically. That atomicity is the whole trick: a reader is always reading a specific, fully committed version of the log, so there's no way to see a half-written state, which is what gives Delta its ACID behavior on top of storage that has no transactions of its own. On schema, the default is enforcement -- if a write shows up with a column Delta doesn't recognize or a type mismatch, it just fails the write, which I actually consider a feature, not an inconvenience, because it stops bad data from silently landing in a table people are relying on. Schema evolution is the deliberate escape hatch -- I pass mergeSchema when writing, and Delta will add that new column to the table going forward, backfilling NULLs for the rows that existed before it showed up. I only turn that on where I actually expect the upstream schema to drift over time, like a semi-structured source feeding a bronze layer -- I wouldn't want it on by default for a curated gold table where an unexpected new column showing up is exactly the kind of thing I want to be alerted to, not silently absorbed.
questions.example:
df.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("mergeSchema", "true").save("/mnt/bronze/orders")
-- Without mergeSchema, a new 'discount_code' column in incoming data causes the write to fail outright.
commonMistakes: Thinking Delta tables are just Parquet files with no additional metadata layer
Not understanding that atomic log commits, not file locking, are what provide ACID guarantees
Enabling mergeSchema by default everywhere, letting uncontrolled schema drift into curated tables
Confusing schema evolution (adding a new column) with schema overwrite (replacing the schema entirely, which needs overwriteSchema)
keyPoints: A Delta table is Parquet files plus an ordered, atomically-committed transaction log
Atomic log commits give readers a consistent, all-or-nothing view of the table's state
Schema enforcement is the default and rejects writes with unexpected columns or types
Schema evolution (mergeSchema) is opt-in and should be reserved for sources expected to drift

deepDive.heading: Optimistic Concurrency and Conflict Resolution
deepDive.content: When two writers attempt to commit at the same time, Delta uses optimistic concurrency control: each writer reads the latest log version it knows about, prepares its change, and tries to commit the next version number atomically. If another writer already claimed that version, the losing writer's commit is rejected and it must re-read the new latest version, re-validate its change against it, and retry. This avoids locking the table for writes while still guaranteeing no two commits silently overwrite each other's intended version.

deepDive.heading: Checkpoints and Log Compaction
deepDive.content: Replaying thousands of individual JSON commit files to reconstruct current table state would get slow over time, so Delta periodically writes a checkpoint -- a Parquet snapshot of the table's full state at a given version. Readers can then start from the nearest checkpoint and only replay the smaller number of JSON commits after it, which is also what keeps Time Travel queries against older versions practical rather than requiring a full log replay from version zero every time.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the transaction log's role in providing ACID guarantees
Correctly explains schema enforcement as the default, rejecting behavior
Correctly explains schema evolution as the opt-in mergeSchema behavior

questions.title: Recursive CTE for an Employee Hierarchy
questions.prompt: Write a recursive CTE that returns every employee under a given manager, at any depth, along with their depth level. Explain what the anchor and recursive members each do.
questions.modelAnswer: A recursive CTE has two parts joined by UNION ALL: an anchor member that defines the starting point of the recursion, and a recursive member that references the CTE itself to repeatedly pull the next level down (or up) until no more rows match. For an employee hierarchy, the anchor member selects the starting manager by EmployeeID, with their depth set to 0. The recursive member joins the Employee table to the CTE itself on Employee.ManagerID = CTE.EmployeeID, pulling in the next level of direct reports and incrementing depth by 1 each pass. SQL Server executes this iteratively: it runs the anchor once, then repeatedly runs the recursive member against the rows produced by the previous iteration, until an iteration produces zero new rows, at which point the recursion stops. A MAXRECURSION hint (default 100) guards against an accidental infinite loop, such as a cyclical ManagerID reference.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd structure it as the classic two-part pattern. The anchor is just 'start here' -- select the one employee I'm rolling the hierarchy from, with depth 0. The recursive part is the interesting half: it joins Employee back to the CTE itself, matching each employee's ManagerID to an EmployeeID already found in the previous pass, and bumps the depth counter by one each time. SQL Server runs this like a loop under the hood -- anchor first, then recursive member against the most recent batch of new rows, over and over, until a pass comes back empty and the whole thing stops. The detail I always double check in a real org chart is MAXRECURSION -- it defaults to 100, which is usually plenty, but if the hierarchy is unusually deep, or if there's a data bug where someone's ManagerID accidentally points back down the chain and creates a cycle, I want that limit to catch it with an error rather than let the query run forever.
questions.example:
WITH OrgChart AS (
  SELECT EmployeeID, ManagerID, Name, 0 AS Depth
  FROM Employee WHERE EmployeeID = 101
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.EmployeeID, e.ManagerID, e.Name, oc.Depth + 1
  FROM Employee e
  JOIN OrgChart oc ON e.ManagerID = oc.EmployeeID
)
SELECT * FROM OrgChart OPTION (MAXRECURSION 50);
commonMistakes: Joining the recursive member to the base table instead of back to the CTE itself
Forgetting UNION ALL is required, not UNION, between the anchor and recursive members
Not guarding against cyclical data with MAXRECURSION, risking an infinite loop
Omitting the depth/level column, making it hard to visually indent or limit the hierarchy later
keyPoints: The anchor member defines the starting row(s) of the recursion
The recursive member joins back to the CTE itself and must use UNION ALL
SQL Server iterates the recursive member until a pass returns zero new rows
MAXRECURSION guards against infinite loops from cyclical hierarchy data

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct anchor member
Writes a correct recursive member joining back to the CTE
Correctly explains the iteration/termination mechanism
Mentions MAXRECURSION as a safeguard

questions.title: PIVOT for a Monthly Sales Crosstab
questions.prompt: You have a table of (Region, Month, SalesAmount) rows and need a crosstab with one row per Region and one column per month. Write the PIVOT query, and explain why the list of month values can't be dynamic without extra work.
questions.modelAnswer: PIVOT rotates distinct values from one column into separate output columns, aggregating as it goes. The syntax requires three things: the aggregate function and the value column being aggregated, the column whose distinct values become new column headers, and an explicit list of exactly which values from that column to turn into columns. That explicit list is the catch -- PIVOT's column list has to be hard-coded in the query text itself; T-SQL has no way to say 'pivot on whatever distinct values happen to exist in this column right now.' If new months are added later and you want them to automatically appear as new columns, static PIVOT won't do that -- you'd need to build the column list dynamically and execute the resulting SQL string with dynamic SQL (sp_executesql), reading the distinct values first and then constructing the PIVOT statement around them at runtime.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this with a plain PIVOT since the months are a known, finite list. The query first needs a derived table or CTE with just the columns I care about -- Region, Month, SalesAmount -- then PIVOT(SUM(SalesAmount) FOR Month IN ([Jan], [Feb], ..., [Dec])) turns the distinct month values into actual columns, aggregated by SUM. The thing I always flag to whoever's asking for this: that column list in the IN(...) clause is static text in the query -- SQL Server has no mechanism to pivot on 'whatever values are in this column today' automatically. If the set of pivot values can genuinely grow -- say, pivoting on ProductCategory instead of a fixed twelve months -- static PIVOT isn't the right tool at all; I'd build the list of distinct values first, concatenate it into a PIVOT statement as a string, and run it with dynamic SQL, which is more code but the only way to make the column set adapt to the data automatically.
commonMistakes: Expecting PIVOT's column list to adapt automatically to new distinct values
Forgetting PIVOT requires an aggregate function even if there's logically only one value per group
Not pre-selecting only the needed columns before PIVOT, causing unexpected extra grouping
Reaching for dynamic SQL immediately instead of a static PIVOT when the value list is actually fixed and known
keyPoints: PIVOT rotates distinct column values into separate output columns using an aggregate
The list of values to pivot on must be written explicitly in the query
A growing or unknown set of pivot values requires dynamic SQL to build the column list at runtime
A derived table/CTE selecting only the relevant columns first avoids unexpected PIVOT grouping

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes correct PIVOT syntax
Correctly explains the static column-list limitation
Correctly describes the dynamic SQL workaround

questions.title: TRY/CATCH With a Multi-Statement Transaction
questions.prompt: Write a stored procedure that transfers a dollar amount between two accounts using two UPDATE statements inside a transaction, with TRY/CATCH ensuring that if either UPDATE fails, both are rolled back and the error is re-raised to the caller.
questions.modelAnswer: The pattern wraps BEGIN TRANSACTION and both UPDATE statements inside a TRY block, and puts the rollback and error-reporting logic inside the matching CATCH block. If any statement in the TRY block raises an error, control jumps immediately to CATCH -- at that point, XACT_STATE() should be checked to see whether the transaction is still in a state that can be rolled back (1 or -1) before calling ROLLBACK TRANSACTION, since calling ROLLBACK on a transaction that's already been auto-rolled-back by SQL Server due to certain error types would itself raise an error. After rolling back, the CATCH block typically captures ERROR_MESSAGE(), ERROR_NUMBER(), ERROR_SEVERITY(), and ERROR_STATE(), and either re-raises the error to the caller using THROW (preserving the original error information) or RAISERROR with the captured details, so the calling application knows the operation failed rather than silently swallowing the error.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd write this with the transaction and both UPDATEs inside the TRY block, and all the cleanup logic inside CATCH. The moment either UPDATE throws, execution jumps straight into CATCH, and the first thing I check there is XACT_STATE() -- if it's -1, SQL Server's already decided the transaction is unrecoverable and only a rollback is allowed; if it's 1, the transaction's still open and rollback is fine; if it's 0, there's nothing to roll back at all. I roll back when appropriate, then I don't just swallow the error -- I re-throw it with THROW so the caller actually finds out the transfer failed, instead of silently returning success. The habit I'd bring to this specifically for a money-transfer-style operation is keeping the transaction scope as tight as possible -- just the two UPDATEs, nothing else slow or unrelated inside it -- because every millisecond that transaction stays open is a millisecond those account rows are locked for everyone else.
commonMistakes: Calling ROLLBACK unconditionally without checking XACT_STATE(), causing an additional error on an already-doomed transaction
Swallowing the error in CATCH without re-raising it, so the caller thinks the transfer succeeded
Putting unrelated, slow logic inside the transaction scope, extending lock duration unnecessarily
Forgetting that THROW with no parameters must be the first statement in the CATCH block to re-raise the original error correctly
keyPoints: TRY wraps the transaction and statements that might fail
CATCH checks XACT_STATE() before deciding whether ROLLBACK is safe to call
THROW re-raises the original error so the caller is informed of failure
Transaction scope should be kept as short as possible to minimize lock duration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes correct TRY/CATCH structure around the transaction
Correctly uses XACT_STATE() before rolling back
Correctly re-raises the error to the caller
Keeps the transaction scope tight

questions.title: Designing a Covering Index
questions.prompt: A query filters on OrderDate and returns CustomerID, OrderDate, and TotalDue, running thousands of times a day. Design an index that lets this query avoid a key lookup entirely, and explain the role of the INCLUDE clause versus adding every column to the index key.
questions.modelAnswer: A covering index contains every column the query needs -- both the filter columns and the output columns -- so the engine can satisfy the whole query from the index alone, without a key lookup back to the clustered index for columns the index itself doesn't have. Here, the index key should be OrderDate, since that's the filter and benefits from being seekable, and CustomerID and TotalDue should go in the INCLUDE clause rather than the key. The distinction matters: key columns determine the sort order of the index and affect how selective a seek is, and adding non-filtering columns to the key can bloat the key size and change sort behavior unnecessarily, while INCLUDE columns are stored at the leaf level alongside the key but don't participate in sorting or the key's uniqueness -- they're purely there to be returned without a lookup. CREATE INDEX IX_Order_OrderDate ON [Order](OrderDate) INCLUDE (CustomerID, TotalDue) gives a seek on OrderDate and returns the other two columns directly from the index leaf pages, eliminating the key lookup entirely for this specific query shape.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd put OrderDate as the key column, since that's what the query actually filters and seeks on, and CustomerID and TotalDue in INCLUDE, since the query just needs to read those values back without filtering or sorting by them. The reason I wouldn't just throw all three into the key is that key columns affect the index's sort order and its size at every level of the B-tree, not just the leaf -- padding the key with columns that don't need to be there makes the index wider and less efficient for no benefit. INCLUDE columns get stored right alongside the key at the leaf level, so the engine can hand back CustomerID and TotalDue directly from the same index pages it's already seeking into, without a second trip back to the clustered index to fetch them -- that second trip, the key lookup, is exactly the cost this index design eliminates. Running thousands of times a day, that's a meaningful difference: it's the gap between a single efficient seek-plus-return and a seek followed by a lookup for every single row.
questions.example:
CREATE INDEX IX_Order_OrderDate_Covering
ON [Order] (OrderDate)
INCLUDE (CustomerID, TotalDue);
-- SELECT CustomerID, OrderDate, TotalDue FROM [Order] WHERE OrderDate = '2026-11-01' now resolves entirely from this index, no key lookup.
commonMistakes: Putting every needed column into the index key instead of using INCLUDE for non-filtering columns
Forgetting a key lookup is still a real per-row cost, not negligible on a high-frequency query
Creating a covering index for a query that's rarely run, adding write overhead for little benefit
Not checking the actual execution plan to confirm the key lookup is actually gone after the change
keyPoints: A covering index satisfies the entire query from the index alone, avoiding a key lookup
Filter/seek columns belong in the index key; columns only needed in the output belong in INCLUDE
INCLUDE columns don't affect sort order or index size at non-leaf levels
The benefit scales with query frequency, which matters for a query running thousands of times a day

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Designs a correct covering index with the right key/INCLUDE split
Correctly explains the difference between key and INCLUDE columns
Explains the key lookup elimination benefit

questions.title: Stored Procedure With a Table-Valued Parameter for Bulk Upsert
questions.prompt: You need a stored procedure that accepts a batch of 500 product price updates in one call and upserts them, instead of calling a single-row procedure 500 times. Write it using a table-valued parameter and MERGE.
questions.modelAnswer: A table-valued parameter (TVP) lets you pass an entire result set into a stored procedure as a single parameter, backed by a user-defined table type that must be created first with CREATE TYPE. The calling application populates a DataTable (or equivalent) matching that type's shape and passes it in one round trip, instead of making 500 separate network calls -- which is the real performance win here, since round-trip latency, not the database work itself, usually dominates a loop of 500 single-row calls. Inside the procedure, the TVP behaves like a read-only table you can reference directly in a MERGE statement: MERGE INTO Product AS target USING @PriceUpdates AS source ON target.ProductID = source.ProductID, WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE, WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT. One detail worth knowing: a TVP is read-only inside the procedure by default -- you cannot UPDATE, INSERT, or DELETE rows within the parameter itself, only read from it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The performance argument for this is almost entirely about round trips, not raw database throughput -- 500 single-row calls means 500 separate network round trips and 500 separate transaction/compile overheads, while a TVP collapses all of that into one call. I'd start by creating a user-defined table type matching the shape of the incoming batch -- ProductID and NewPrice, say -- then write the procedure to accept that type as a read-only parameter. Inside, I treat the parameter just like any other table and feed it straight into a MERGE against the real Product table: match on ProductID, UPDATE the price when matched, INSERT a new row when not. The one thing I'd flag to someone new to TVPs: you can't modify the TVP itself inside the procedure -- it's strictly read-only, so if you need a working copy to manipulate, you'd first copy it into a #temp table.
commonMistakes: Calling a single-row procedure in a loop instead of batching with a TVP, multiplying network round trips
Forgetting the TVP must be declared READONLY and trying to modify it inside the procedure
Not creating a matching index or primary key on the table type when the batch size could be large
Omitting a WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE clause when stale rows genuinely need to be removed, versus just upserted
keyPoints: A table-valued parameter passes an entire batch into a procedure in one call
A user-defined table type must be created first to define the TVP's shape
TVPs are read-only inside the procedure by default
MERGE against the TVP handles the upsert logic in a single statement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Creates a correct table type and TVP parameter
Writes a correct MERGE statement using the TVP
Explains the round-trip performance benefit over looping

questions.title: Implementing SCD Type 2 With MERGE
questions.prompt: Write the T-SQL MERGE logic for a Type 2 slowly changing dimension on DimCustomer, where a change to Address should close out the current row (set EndDate, IsCurrent = 0) and insert a new current row, while an unchanged customer should be left alone.
questions.modelAnswer: A true Type 2 SCD update actually needs two passes, because a single MERGE statement can't both close an existing row and insert a brand-new row for the same business key in one WHEN clause. The first MERGE compares incoming source rows to the current (IsCurrent = 1) dimension rows on the natural/business key, and where a tracked attribute like Address differs, it sets EndDate = current date and IsCurrent = 0 on the existing row (a WHEN MATCHED ... AND changed THEN UPDATE). The second pass is an INSERT of new current rows -- for brand-new customers not yet in the dimension at all, and for existing customers whose attribute just changed and need a new current row with a new surrogate key, EffectiveDate = current date, EndDate = NULL, IsCurrent = 1. The key design point is that the surrogate key (CustomerKey) changes with every new version, while the natural/business key (CustomerID) stays the same across versions, which is what lets fact tables joined to the historical version remain pointed at the correct point-in-time attribute values.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always explain up front that this isn't a single-statement operation, even though MERGE makes it tempting to think it could be -- closing an old row and inserting its replacement are fundamentally different actions on different rows, and MERGE's WHEN clauses operate per matched row, not 'update this row and also insert a different one.' So I do it in two steps. First, a MERGE (or a plain UPDATE) against DimCustomer where IsCurrent = 1, comparing the incoming Address to what's on file -- if it changed, I close that row out: EndDate = today, IsCurrent = 0. Second, an INSERT that picks up both brand-new customers and customers whose row I just closed, giving each a new surrogate CustomerKey, EffectiveDate = today, EndDate = NULL, IsCurrent = 1. The detail that matters for the rest of the warehouse: CustomerID, the natural key, never changes across versions, but CustomerKey does -- that's exactly what lets a historical fact row stay joined to the customer's old address while a current fact row joins to the new one.
questions.example:
-- Step 1: close changed rows
UPDATE d SET EndDate = GETDATE(), IsCurrent = 0
FROM DimCustomer d JOIN StagingCustomer s ON d.CustomerID = s.CustomerID
WHERE d.IsCurrent = 1 AND d.Address <> s.Address;

-- Step 2: insert new current rows (new customers + changed customers)
INSERT INTO DimCustomer (CustomerID, Address, EffectiveDate, EndDate, IsCurrent)
SELECT s.CustomerID, s.Address, GETDATE(), NULL, 1
FROM StagingCustomer s
LEFT JOIN DimCustomer d ON s.CustomerID = d.CustomerID AND d.IsCurrent = 1
WHERE d.CustomerID IS NULL;
commonMistakes: Trying to do the close-out and the new-row insert in a single MERGE statement's WHEN MATCHED clause
Reusing the same surrogate key for the new version instead of generating a new one
Comparing every column for a change instead of only the attributes actually tracked for history
Forgetting to also catch brand-new customers that don't exist in the dimension at all yet
keyPoints: SCD Type 2 requires closing the old row and inserting a new row as two distinct operations
The natural/business key stays constant; the surrogate key changes with each new version
Only tracked attributes should trigger a new version, not every column difference
New customers and changed customers both need an insert into the current-row set

deepDive.heading: Handling Multiple Tracked Attributes Cleanly
deepDive.content: When more than one attribute is tracked for history (Address, Tier, SalesRegion), compare them with a single composite condition using CHECKSUM, HASHBYTES, or simply OR-ing individual comparisons, and store that comparison result as a computed RowHash column on the dimension. Comparing a precomputed hash instead of several individual column comparisons each time keeps the change-detection logic fast and makes it trivial to add a new tracked attribute later without rewriting the comparison predicate everywhere it appears.

deepDive.heading: Fact Table Join Strategy Across SCD Versions
deepDive.content: Fact rows should be loaded using a lookup against the dimension's EffectiveDate/EndDate range for the transaction's date, not simply joining to IsCurrent = 1, so that a historical transaction permanently reflects the customer attributes that were true at the time it happened. This is also why ETL load order matters: the dimension must be fully updated for a given business date before fact rows for that date are loaded against it.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the two-step close-then-insert pattern
Writes correct SQL for both steps
Correctly distinguishes natural key from surrogate key behavior

questions.title: Parsing Semi-Structured JSON With OPENJSON
questions.prompt: A column in a staging table stores a JSON array of line items per order, like [{"sku":"A1","qty":2},{"sku":"B4","qty":1}]. Write a query that shreds this into one row per line item, joined back to the order's OrderID.
questions.modelAnswer: OPENJSON parses a JSON text value and returns it as a rowset, which can be consumed directly or shaped with an explicit schema using the WITH clause. For a JSON array, each array element becomes one row, and WITH lets you define typed output columns mapped to JSON paths within each element -- here, sku as a string and qty as an int. CROSS APPLY is the right join operator to use against the staging table, because OPENJSON needs to be evaluated once per row of the outer table (once per order's JSON text), and CROSS APPLY allows the right-hand table-valued function to reference a column from the left-hand table, which a plain JOIN cannot do. The result is one row per line item per order, each row still carrying the originating OrderID from the outer table alongside the shredded sku and qty values.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for OPENJSON with an explicit WITH clause rather than the default untyped output, because I want strongly typed sku and qty columns coming straight out of the function instead of having to cast everything afterward. The join has to be CROSS APPLY, not a regular JOIN -- OPENJSON is a table-valued function, and it needs to see the current row's JSON column as its input, which only works if the function call can reference the outer table's column, and that's exactly what CROSS APPLY allows and a plain JOIN doesn't. Once that's wired up, I get one row per line item, each one still tagged with its OrderID from the outer table, which is the shape I need to then insert into a proper OrderLineItem table instead of leaving the data buried as JSON text in staging.
questions.example:
SELECT o.OrderID, j.sku, j.qty
FROM StagingOrder o
CROSS APPLY OPENJSON(o.LineItemsJson)
  WITH (sku VARCHAR(20) '$.sku', qty INT '$.qty') AS j;
commonMistakes: Using a plain JOIN instead of CROSS APPLY, which fails because OPENJSON can't reference the outer row's column that way
Skipping the WITH clause and getting generic key/value/type columns instead of properly typed output
Not validating the JSON with ISJSON() first, risking an error on malformed rows
Forgetting nested JSON objects inside the array need their own nested WITH clause or a second OPENJSON pass
keyPoints: OPENJSON shreds JSON text into a rowset, one row per array element
The WITH clause defines typed output columns mapped to JSON paths
CROSS APPLY is required so OPENJSON can reference the outer table's JSON column per row
ISJSON() is a useful guard before parsing JSON from an untrusted or inconsistent source column

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct OPENJSON WITH clause
Correctly uses CROSS APPLY and explains why
Produces the correct one-row-per-line-item output shape

questions.title: DAX Time Intelligence: YTD vs. Same Period Last Year
questions.prompt: Write a DAX measure for Year-to-Date Sales and a separate measure comparing current sales to the same period last year, and explain the one precondition both measures silently depend on.
