questions.modelAnswer: TOTALYTD(SUM(Sales[Amount]), 'Date'[Date]) calculates the running total of sales from the start of the current fiscal year up through the latest date in the current filter context, and SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date]) shifts the current date filter context back exactly one year, which CALCULATE then uses to re-evaluate the sales measure against that shifted period. Both of these, and essentially every DAX time intelligence function, silently depend on having a proper date dimension table marked as a Date Table in the model (via Mark as Date Table, or implicitly through a continuous, gap-free date column), related to the fact table on a date key. Without a contiguous calendar table covering every date in the relevant range -- not just the dates that happen to appear in the fact table -- these functions can produce silently wrong results, because they work by generating a date range internally and expect the date column to behave like a real calendar, not a sparse list of transaction dates.
questions.professionalAnswer: YTD Sales = TOTALYTD(SUM(Sales[Amount]), 'Date'[Date]) and Sales SPLY = CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date])) are the two measures. The thing I always check before trusting either of them in a new model is whether there's a real, dedicated date dimension table, marked explicitly as a date table, with one row for every single calendar date in the full range the data covers -- not a date column pulled straight off the fact table with gaps wherever there happened to be no transactions. Time intelligence functions like these generate their date ranges by assuming the date column behaves like a real, continuous calendar; if it's missing dates, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR and TOTALYTD can quietly return wrong numbers with no error at all, which is a much worse failure mode than an outright error, because nothing visibly breaks to tell you to go check.
questions.example: A model using the raw OrderDate column from the Sales fact table as its 'date' for time intelligence, with no separate Date table, returns incorrect SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR results for any day with zero transactions last year, because that date simply doesn't exist in the column being used.
commonMistakes: Using the fact table's transaction date column directly instead of a proper, continuous date dimension
Forgetting to mark the date table as a Date Table in the model relationships
Assuming time intelligence functions validate date continuity and will error if it's missing, when they just silently return wrong numbers
Mixing fiscal year settings between TOTALYTD's optional year-end parameter and the rest of the model inconsistently
keyPoints: TOTALYTD computes a running total from the start of the year to the current filter context's latest date
SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR shifts the date filter context back exactly one year for CALCULATE to re-evaluate against
Both functions require a contiguous, dedicated date dimension table marked as a Date Table
A gap-filled or missing date table causes silent, not obvious, incorrect results

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct YTD measure
Writes a correct same-period-last-year measure
Correctly identifies the date table precondition
Explains the silent-failure risk if the precondition is unmet

questions.title: Row-Level Security With a Role-Playing Date Dimension
questions.prompt: You need to implement RLS in Power BI so regional managers only see their own region's data, in a model where a single Date table plays two roles: OrderDate and ShipDate, with only one active relationship. Describe how you'd set up the RLS role, and how USERELATIONSHIP fits in if a measure needs to force the inactive ShipDate relationship.
questions.modelAnswer: RLS is set up by creating a role in Manage Roles with a DAX filter expression on the table holding the region attribute -- typically [Region] = USERNAME() or, more robustly, a mapping table joining login identities to allowed regions via LOOKUPVALUE, so access can be managed without hardcoding emails into the model. That role filter propagates automatically across any active relationship from the filtered table outward, which is unrelated to the role-playing dimension question but matters for a different reason: when a single Date table serves two purposes (OrderDate and ShipDate) against a fact table, only one of those two relationships can be active at a time, because a model can't have two simultaneously active paths between the same pair of tables without creating ambiguity. The inactive relationship (say, ShipDate) still exists and can be used, but only when a specific measure explicitly invokes it via USERELATIONSHIP inside a CALCULATE call, which temporarily activates that specific relationship for the duration of that one calculation, without changing which relationship is active by default for every other measure in the model.
questions.professionalAnswer: The RLS setup itself is separate from the role-playing dimension issue, so I'd address them as two distinct pieces. For RLS, I'd create a role with a DAX filter on the Region column -- ideally not a hardcoded USERNAME() = 'x' per region, but a small mapping table of login to allowed region(s), filtered with something like [Region] IN VALUES via LOOKUPVALUE, so adding a new manager doesn't mean editing the model. That role filter flows automatically through active relationships once it's applied to the right table. The role-playing Date table is a separate modeling reality: since only one relationship between Date and the fact table can be active, OrderDate is probably the one carrying the default, while ShipDate sits there inactive but not unusable. Any measure that specifically needs to analyze by ship date has to explicitly say so with CALCULATE(..., USERELATIONSHIP(Fact[ShipDateKey], Date[DateKey])), which activates that one relationship just for that calculation -- it doesn't change the model's default active relationship, it just overrides it locally for that specific measure's evaluation.
questions.example:
Sales by Ship Date =
CALCULATE(
    SUM(Sales[Amount]),
    USERELATIONSHIP(Sales[ShipDateKey], 'Date'[DateKey])
)
-- Forces the otherwise-inactive ShipDate relationship for this one measure only.
commonMistakes: Hardcoding USERNAME() comparisons per region instead of using a maintainable mapping table
Forgetting only one relationship between a role-playing dimension and a fact table can be active by default
Assuming USERELATIONSHIP changes the model's default active relationship globally instead of just for that one calculation
Not testing RLS roles with 'View As Roles' before publishing, missing a region with no data returned at all
keyPoints: RLS roles use a DAX filter expression, ideally backed by a maintainable mapping table
A role-playing dimension can only have one active relationship to a given fact table at a time
USERELATIONSHIP activates an inactive relationship for the scope of a single CALCULATE call
RLS filters propagate through whichever relationship is active, independent of the USERELATIONSHIP question

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes setting up an RLS role with a DAX filter
Correctly explains the single active relationship constraint
Correctly explains USERELATIONSHIP's scope and usage

questions.title: Tableau Table Calculation Addressing and Partitioning
questions.prompt: You built a running total table calculation in Tableau, but it resets incorrectly when you add a new dimension to the view. Explain addressing versus partitioning fields, and how Compute Using lets you fix this.
questions.modelAnswer: A table calculation runs against the dimensions in the current view, and every dimension in that view gets sorted into one of two roles: addressing fields, which define the direction the calculation moves across (the order it 'walks' through values, like a running total moving across Month), and partitioning fields, which define the separate, independent groups the calculation restarts within (like Region, if you want the running total to reset at the start of each region). By default, Tableau decides this split automatically based on the order dimensions appear in the view, which is exactly why adding a new dimension to the view -- even one you intended to just be a label or additional grouping -- can silently shift which fields are addressing and which are partitioning, causing the running total to reset at a new, unintended boundary. Compute Using (or the more explicit Edit Table Calculation dialog) lets you override that automatic assignment directly: you choose exactly which field(s) should be addressing (the calculation walks across them) and which should be left as partitioning (the calculation restarts for each combination of them), regardless of how Tableau would have guessed based on the view's current layout.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is one of those Tableau behaviors that looks like a bug the first time it happens, but it's actually the automatic addressing/partitioning logic doing exactly what it's designed to do, just not what I wanted. Every dimension in the view gets bucketed as either addressing -- the direction the calculation steps through -- or partitioning -- the boundary it restarts at. By default Tableau infers this from the order of dimensions in the view, so dropping in a new dimension, even one I just wanted for extra detail, can quietly reassign that split and change where my running total resets. The fix is to stop letting Tableau guess -- right-click the calculation, go to Edit Table Calculation, and explicitly set Compute Using to specify exactly which field is addressing (say, Month, so the running total walks forward in time) and which stays as partitioning (Region, so each region's running total restarts independently). Once I set that explicitly, adding more dimensions to the view for other reasons doesn't silently break the calculation anymore, because I've pinned down its behavior instead of relying on Tableau's layout-order guess.
questions.example: A running total of Sales computed across Month, partitioned by Region: each region's total restarts at the first month and accumulates forward independently of every other region's running total, because Month is set as the addressing field and Region as the partitioning field via Compute Using.
commonMistakes: Assuming a table calculation's addressing/partitioning assignment is fixed once set, rather than re-derived automatically as the view changes
Adding a new dimension to a view without checking whether it silently changed a table calculation's behavior
Not using the explicit Edit Table Calculation dialog to pin addressing/partitioning when the calculation is business-critical
Confusing table calculation partitioning with LOD expression dimensions, which are a completely separate mechanism
keyPoints: Addressing fields define the direction a table calculation steps through
Partitioning fields define the independent groups a table calculation restarts within
Tableau infers this split automatically from the view's dimension order by default
Compute Using lets you explicitly override which fields are addressing versus partitioning

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains addressing vs. partitioning
Correctly explains why adding a dimension broke the calculation
Correctly describes the Compute Using fix

questions.title: Handling Schema Drift in an ADF Mapping Data Flow
questions.prompt: A source CSV feed occasionally adds or renames columns without warning, and your ADF mapping data flow currently breaks whenever that happens. Explain how to configure the data flow to tolerate schema drift, and the tradeoff of doing so.
questions.modelAnswer: By default, a mapping data flow's source transformation expects a fixed, projected schema, and any column that appears, disappears, or gets renamed in the actual source file breaks that fixed mapping. Enabling 'Allow schema drift' on the source transformation tells the data flow to accept whatever columns actually show up at runtime rather than enforcing the originally-projected schema, and 'Infer drifted column types' lets it guess reasonable data types for any new columns it encounters instead of treating them all as strings. Downstream transformations can then reference drifted columns dynamically using pattern-based column matching (byName(), byPosition(), or rule-based mapping with regex column patterns) rather than listing every column by its exact original name, so a sink can still write out columns that weren't known when the pipeline was built. The tradeoff is reduced predictability and weaker validation: a genuinely unexpected or malformed new column now flows through silently instead of failing loudly, so a schema-drift-tolerant pipeline usually needs its own separate validation step -- checking row counts, expected column presence, or data quality rules -- to catch problems that strict schema enforcement used to catch for free.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd turn on Allow Schema Drift on the source transformation specifically, which stops the data flow from hard-failing the moment the source's actual columns don't match what was originally mapped. Pairing that with Infer Drifted Column Types means new columns get a reasonable guessed type instead of defaulting to string for everything, which saves a lot of manual casting downstream. The part that actually takes real work is making sure the rest of the data flow doesn't just break in a different place -- any transformation or sink mapping that referenced columns by their exact original name needs to switch to pattern-based matching, like byName() patterns or rule-based column mapping, so it can pick up a renamed or newly added column without someone manually updating the pipeline every time the source changes. The tradeoff I always bring up to whoever owns this pipeline: tolerating drift means a genuinely bad or unexpected new column now flows through quietly instead of failing the pipeline outright, so I'd pair this with a separate validation step downstream -- checking that expected core columns are still present, row counts look sane -- because strict schema enforcement was accidentally doing some of that data-quality checking for free before.
questions.example: A vendor renames 'CustID' to 'CustomerID' in their export; with schema drift enabled and a rule-based column mapping using a regex pattern matching both possible names, the pipeline keeps running instead of failing on a missing expected column.
commonMistakes: Enabling Allow Schema Drift but leaving downstream mappings referencing exact original column names, which still break
Not pairing drift tolerance with a separate data-quality validation step
Assuming Infer Drifted Column Types always guesses the correct data type for ambiguous new columns
Turning on schema drift everywhere by default instead of only on sources that genuinely need it
keyPoints: Allow Schema Drift on the source lets the data flow accept columns not in the original projected schema
Infer Drifted Column Types assigns reasonable data types to new columns automatically
Downstream transformations need pattern-based column mapping to actually use drifted columns
Schema drift tolerance trades strict validation for resilience, requiring a separate data-quality check

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes enabling schema drift and type inference
Correctly explains the need for pattern-based downstream mapping
Correctly articulates the validation tradeoff

questions.title: Snowflake Bulk Loading With COPY INTO and ON_ERROR
questions.prompt: Write a COPY INTO statement that loads CSV files from a Snowflake stage into a table, skipping any file that has more than a small number of malformed rows rather than failing the whole load, and explain how you'd find out afterward which rows were skipped.
questions.modelAnswer: COPY INTO's ON_ERROR option controls how the load reacts to a malformed row: ON_ERROR = 'ABORT_STATEMENT' (the default) fails the entire load on the first error, ON_ERROR = 'CONTINUE' skips just the bad row and keeps loading everything else, and ON_ERROR = 'SKIP_FILE_<n>' skips an entire file once it accumulates more than n errors, which is the right choice when a handful of malformed rows in one file suggest a data quality issue worth flagging but shouldn't block files that load cleanly. After the load, COPY INTO's own result output and the load history don't show the specific skipped rows in detail by default, so VALIDATE(table_name, JOB_ID => '_last') or querying the COPY_HISTORY / LOAD_HISTORY metadata functions is the way to retrieve the specific error details -- which row, which column, and what the parsing error was -- for a completed load, and VALIDATION_MODE can also be used on the COPY INTO statement itself to do a dry-run validation pass before committing to the actual load.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set ON_ERROR = 'SKIP_FILE_5' or similar, rather than the default ABORT_STATEMENT, since the ask here is specifically 'tolerate a few bad rows per file, but if a file's clearly a mess, skip the whole thing rather than silently loading half of it.' ABORT_STATEMENT would be too strict -- one bad row anywhere kills the entire batch -- and plain CONTINUE would quietly load every file no matter how bad, which isn't what's being asked for either. Once the load's done, I wouldn't expect the row-level detail to just be sitting in the COPY INTO output -- I'd run VALIDATE(table_name, JOB_ID => '_last') right after, which gives me the specific rows and errors from that most recent load, or query COPY_HISTORY for a load that happened further in the past. If I wanted to catch problems before committing to the real load at all, I'd also run the same COPY INTO with VALIDATION_MODE set, which does a dry run and reports what would have failed without actually loading anything.
commonMistakes: Leaving ON_ERROR at the default ABORT_STATEMENT and having one bad row fail an entire multi-file load
Using CONTINUE when the intent is actually to reject an entire bad file, not just skip individual rows
Assuming the COPY INTO command output itself lists every skipped row's details
Not using VALIDATION_MODE to dry-run a load before committing to it on a new or unreliable source feed
keyPoints: ON_ERROR controls row/file-level tolerance: ABORT_STATEMENT, CONTINUE, or SKIP_FILE_<n>
SKIP_FILE_<n> is the right choice for tolerating a few errors per file but rejecting clearly bad files
VALIDATE() or COPY_HISTORY retrieves the specific error detail from a completed load
VALIDATION_MODE allows a dry-run check before committing to an actual load

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct COPY INTO statement with the appropriate ON_ERROR setting
Correctly explains the difference between ON_ERROR options
Correctly describes how to retrieve skipped-row detail afterward

questions.title: A dbt Incremental Model With a Unique Key
questions.prompt: Write a dbt incremental model for a fct_orders table that should only process new or updated rows based on an updated_at timestamp, and correctly handle a customer who updates the same order twice before the next run.
questions.modelAnswer: An incremental model needs {{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='order_id') }} at the top, which tells dbt both to only append/merge rather than rebuild the whole table on subsequent runs, and which column identifies a row that might already exist and need updating rather than inserting as a duplicate. The is_incremental() macro wraps a WHERE clause that's only applied on incremental runs (not the very first full build): WHERE updated_at > (SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM {{ this }}) limits the source scan to only rows that changed since the last run. For the case of the same order_id being updated twice before the next dbt run, dbt's default incremental strategy (merge, on warehouses that support it, like Snowflake or Databricks) handles this correctly as long as the SELECT in the model only returns the latest version of each order_id per run -- which usually means the staging query itself needs its own deduplication logic (like a ROW_NUMBER() QUALIFY = 1 pick of the latest updated_at per order_id) before the incremental merge logic ever sees it, because MERGE matches on unique_key and will simply be confused by two source rows claiming the same key in one run.
questions.professionalAnswer: The model config is the easy part: materialized='incremental', unique_key='order_id', and a WHERE updated_at > max(updated_at from this table) inside an is_incremental() block so that filter only kicks in after the very first full build. The part people often get wrong is the double-update-before-next-run scenario -- if the same order gets touched twice between dbt runs, my source query for that run could return two rows with the same order_id, and that's a real problem for a MERGE-based incremental strategy, because merge matching on unique_key doesn't know what to do with two source rows claiming the same key in the same batch. So before the incremental logic ever runs, I make sure my select is already deduplicated down to one row per order_id -- using QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1, or an equivalent dedup CTE -- so by the time dbt's merge logic runs, there's exactly one row per key, representing its very latest state, and the update behaves correctly either way.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to deduplicate the source query, letting two same-key rows reach the merge in one batch
Not wrapping the incremental filter in is_incremental(), breaking the very first full-refresh build
Filtering on MAX(updated_at) without a small safety overlap window, risking missed late-arriving rows at the boundary
Choosing unique_key incorrectly, such as a non-unique business column instead of the true grain of the table
keyPoints: materialized='incremental' with a unique_key enables merge-style updates on subsequent runs
is_incremental() scopes the filtering logic to only run after the first full build
Source deduplication to one row per key is required before the merge logic runs correctly
unique_key must match the true grain of the table to avoid incorrect merges

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct incremental model config and is_incremental() filter
Correctly identifies and fixes the double-update deduplication problem
Chooses an appropriate unique_key

questions.title: Idempotent MERGE INTO Upsert in Databricks
questions.prompt: Write a Delta Lake MERGE INTO statement that upserts a batch of customer updates into a dim_customer table, and explain what makes this operation safe to re-run if the job fails partway through and gets retried.
questions.modelAnswer: MERGE INTO target USING source ON target.customer_id = source.customer_id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT * matches incoming rows to existing rows by a business key and applies the right action per row in a single atomic operation. What makes it idempotent -- safe to run twice with the same input -- is that matching on customer_id means re-running the exact same batch produces the exact same end state: rows that already match get updated to the same values again (a no-op in effect), and rows that already exist are never re-inserted as duplicates, because the WHEN NOT MATCHED branch only fires for keys genuinely absent from the target. This is fundamentally different from a plain INSERT-based load, which would create duplicate rows every time it's re-run, since INSERT has no concept of 'this key already exists, don't add it again.' The operation is also atomic at the Delta transaction log level -- if the job fails partway through the MERGE itself, Delta's transaction log ensures the table reflects either the complete pre-MERGE state or the complete post-MERGE state, never a partially-applied merge, so a retry starts from a known-clean state rather than a half-applied one.
questions.professionalAnswer: The MERGE statement matches on customer_id, updates existing matches, and inserts anything new -- the key design choice that makes this safe to retry is matching on a stable business key rather than just blindly appending rows. If the exact same batch gets fed through MERGE twice because a retry happened after a failure, the second run doesn't create duplicates or double-count anything -- rows that matched the first time just get updated to the same values again, which is a no-op in practice, and nothing new gets inserted a second time because those keys are already present. That's the real difference between MERGE and a naive append-only INSERT, which would happily create a second copy of every row if you ran it twice. On top of that, Delta's transaction log gives the MERGE itself atomicity -- if the job dies mid-write, the table is left at either the state before the MERGE started or the state after it fully completed, never something in between, so when the orchestrator retries the job, it's retrying against a clean, known starting point rather than a corrupted partial state.
questions.example:
MERGE INTO dim_customer AS target
USING staged_customer_updates AS source
ON target.customer_id = source.customer_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;
commonMistakes: Using a plain INSERT instead of MERGE for an upsert, creating duplicates on every retry
Matching on a non-unique or unstable column instead of a true business key
Assuming idempotency comes from the batch job's orchestration layer rather than from the MERGE logic itself
Not considering that WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * will overwrite every column, even ones a partial source update didn't intend to touch
keyPoints: MERGE INTO matches on a business key and applies update/insert per row in one atomic operation
Matching on a stable key makes re-running the same batch produce the same end state (idempotency)
This differs fundamentally from append-only INSERT, which duplicates rows on retry
Delta's transaction log makes the MERGE itself atomic, so a mid-failure retry starts clean

deepDive.heading: Handling Deletes in the Same Upsert
deepDive.content: A full CDC-style sync often also needs WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE, which removes target rows that no longer appear in the source batch at all -- useful for a full daily snapshot load, but dangerous for a true incremental/CDC feed where the source batch is only a partial delta, since every row absent from that partial batch would get incorrectly deleted. Whether to include this clause depends entirely on whether the source represents the full current state or only a delta of changes.

deepDive.heading: Concurrent Writers and MERGE Conflicts
deepDive.content: If two MERGE operations against the same Delta table run concurrently and their row ranges overlap, Delta's optimistic concurrency control will cause one of them to fail and need to retry against the newer table version, rather than silently corrupting data. Designing upsert jobs to run sequentially per table, or partitioning concurrent jobs so their key ranges never overlap, avoids repeated retry failures under load.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct MERGE INTO statement
Correctly explains why matching on a business key makes retries idempotent
Correctly explains the transaction log's role in atomicity on failure

questions.title: Diagnosing a Deadlock From the Deadlock Graph
questions.prompt: Two stored procedures are deadlocking in production, each updating the same two tables but in opposite order. Explain how you'd confirm this from a deadlock graph, and the fix that doesn't involve rewriting the application's transaction logic.
questions.modelAnswer: A deadlock graph (captured via a system_health extended event session or a dedicated extended event on the deadlock graph) shows each participating process, the specific resource (usually a row or key) it holds a lock on, the resource it's waiting to acquire, and the exact query text each process was running. Confirming the classic 'opposite lock order' pattern means tracing that Process A holds a lock on Table1 and is waiting on Table2, while Process B holds a lock on Table2 and is waiting on Table1 -- a circular wait that SQL Server's deadlock monitor detects and resolves by choosing one process as the deadlock victim and rolling it back with error 1205. The fix that doesn't require rewriting application logic is enforcing a consistent lock acquisition order at the database level: if both procedures are forced to touch Table1 before Table2 every time, through a consistent statement order inside each procedure, the circular wait pattern can't form in the first place, since one process will simply wait behind the other rather than both waiting on each other simultaneously. A complementary, lower-effort mitigation is enabling RCSI, which reduces the number of locks taken for readers in the first place, shrinking the window where this kind of conflict can occur, though it doesn't eliminate writer-writer deadlocks like this one.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd pull the deadlock graph first, either from the system_health session that's always running by default or from a dedicated extended event, and read it for exactly this shape: Process A holding a lock Process B wants, and Process B holding a lock Process A wants, on the same two tables. If the graph shows Table1 then Table2 for one process and Table2 then Table1 for the other, that confirms the opposite-order theory immediately -- it's a textbook circular wait. SQL Server's own deadlock monitor already resolves it by killing one process as the victim and rolling it back with a 1205 error, but obviously that's not acceptable behavior in production, just the symptom. Rather than touching either procedure's transaction logic, which is riskier to change under pressure, my first fix is simply reordering the statements inside whichever procedure updates the tables in the 'wrong' order, so both procedures always touch Table1 before Table2 -- once the lock acquisition order is consistent across every caller, the circular wait condition can't form at all, even under heavy concurrent load.
questions.example:
Procedure A: UPDATE Table1 ... then UPDATE Table2 ...
Procedure B (deadlocking): UPDATE Table2 ... then UPDATE Table1 ...
Fix: reorder Procedure B to UPDATE Table1 before Table2, matching Procedure A's lock order.
commonMistakes: Not knowing the system_health extended event session already captures recent deadlock graphs by default
Assuming the deadlock victim's procedure is the one 'at fault' rather than the lock ordering pattern itself
Jumping straight to adding retry logic in the application instead of fixing the underlying lock order
Confusing a deadlock (circular wait, resolved automatically with a kill) with ordinary blocking (one process just waits)
keyPoints: A deadlock graph shows each process's held and awaited resources and query text
The classic pattern is two processes acquiring locks on the same resources in opposite order
SQL Server automatically resolves a deadlock by killing one process as the victim
Enforcing a consistent lock acquisition order across all callers prevents the circular wait entirely

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains how to read a deadlock graph to confirm the pattern
Correctly identifies consistent lock ordering as the fix
Correctly distinguishes a deadlock from ordinary blocking

questions.title: SARGability: Why an Index Isn't Being Used
questions.prompt: A query filters WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2026 and does a full index scan even though OrderDate has an index. Explain why, and rewrite the predicate so the optimizer can seek.
questions.modelAnswer: Wrapping an indexed column in a function -- YEAR(OrderDate) -- makes the predicate non-SARGable, because SQL Server would have to evaluate YEAR() against every single row's OrderDate value before it can know whether that row matches, which means it can't use the index's sorted order to jump directly to matching rows; it has to scan the whole thing and evaluate the function row by row. This is true regardless of which function wraps the column -- YEAR(), CONVERT(), LEFT(), ISNULL() on the filtered column all have the same effect. The fix is to rewrite the predicate as a range comparison directly against the unmodified column: WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2027-01-01'. This is logically equivalent to filtering for the year 2026, but because the column itself is being compared directly, with no function wrapped around it, the optimizer can use the index's B-tree to seek straight to the start of that range and scan only the matching rows, rather than touching every row in the table.
questions.professionalAnswer: The instant I see a function wrapped around a filtered column -- YEAR(), CONVERT(), anything -- I know that's why the index isn't being used, before I even look at the execution plan. The index is built and sorted on the raw OrderDate values; SQL Server can't peek inside YEAR(OrderDate) and still use that sort order, because it would have to actually compute YEAR() for every row first to know if it matches, which means scanning everything regardless of the index. My fix is always the same shape: turn it into a direct range comparison against the unwrapped column -- OrderDate >= '2026-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2027-01-01' instead of YEAR(OrderDate) = 2026. Logically it's the exact same set of rows, but now the predicate is directly comparable against the column as stored, so the optimizer can seek into the index and only touch the rows in that range, instead of evaluating a function against every row in the table first.
questions.example:
-- Non-SARGable: forces a scan, function wraps the indexed column
WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2026

-- SARGable: allows a seek, direct range comparison on the raw column
WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2027-01-01'
commonMistakes: Wrapping any filtered, indexed column in a function and being surprised the index isn't used
Assuming only YEAR()/date functions cause this, when ISNULL, CONVERT, LEFT, and arithmetic on a column all do too
Rewriting to a range but using <= on the upper bound, accidentally including an extra day/value
Not checking the actual execution plan to confirm a seek replaced the scan after the rewrite
keyPoints: A function wrapped around a filtered column makes the predicate non-SARGable
Non-SARGable predicates force a scan because the optimizer can't use the index's sort order
Rewriting as a direct range comparison on the raw column restores seekability
This applies to any function wrapping the column, not just date functions

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why the function wrapper causes a scan
Writes a correct, logically equivalent SARGable rewrite
Notes this generalizes to other functions, not just YEAR()

questions.title: Troubleshooting a Bidirectional Filtering Ambiguity Warning
questions.prompt: You try to set a relationship's cross-filter direction to Both in Power BI and get a warning about ambiguity, or a measure starts returning unexpectedly inflated numbers after you do. Explain what's actually going wrong and how you'd resolve it.
questions.modelAnswer: A bidirectional (Both) cross-filter relationship lets a filter applied to either side of the relationship propagate to the other, rather than only flowing one direction (typically dimension to fact). The ambiguity warning or inflated-numbers symptom shows up when the model has more than one path between two tables -- commonly a snowflaked or multi-fact-table model -- and setting a relationship to Both creates two or more valid ways for a filter to reach the same table, so the engine can't determine a single, unambiguous route for the filter to travel, and Power BI either blocks the change outright with a warning or, in cases it does allow, silently double-counts rows that get touched by the filter arriving via multiple paths simultaneously. The resolution is almost always to avoid Both relationships in a model with more than two tables unless the ambiguity is deliberately and carefully managed: either keep relationships single-direction and use CALCULATE with CROSSFILTER() inside a specific measure to apply bidirectional behavior only where it's actually needed, or resolve the ambiguity at the model level by consolidating the multiple paths into one, such as flattening a snowflake into a star schema so there's only ever one path between any two tables.
questions.professionalAnswer: Bidirectional filtering ambiguity almost always means the model has more than one way to get from one table to another, and flipping a relationship to Both just exposes that structural problem rather than causing it. If I've got, say, two fact tables both related to a shared dimension, and I also directly relate the two fact tables to each other, setting any of those relationships to Both creates two valid filter paths to the same place, and Power BI can't pick one on its own -- either it stops me with a warning, or worse, it lets the change through and I start seeing numbers that look multiplied, because a filter is reaching the same rows twice via two different routes. My default fix is to not use Both at all in a model with more than a simple two-table shape -- I'd keep every relationship single-direction, and if I genuinely need bidirectional behavior for one specific calculation, I'd scope it narrowly with CALCULATE(..., CROSSFILTER(Table1[Key], Table2[Key], Both)) inside just that one measure, rather than changing the relationship's default behavior for the whole model. If the ambiguity is really structural -- a snowflake with multiple paths -- the cleaner long-term fix is flattening the model into a proper star schema so there's exactly one path between any two tables to begin with.
questions.example:
CROSSFILTER-scoped fix instead of a model-wide Both relationship:
Sales YTD With Promo Filter =
CALCULATE(SUM(Sales[Amount]), CROSSFILTER(Promotion[PromoKey], Sales[PromoKey], BOTH))
commonMistakes: Setting a relationship to Both without checking whether the model already has multiple paths between tables
Not noticing silently inflated numbers because the model let the ambiguous Both relationship through without a warning
Using a model-wide Both relationship when a scoped CROSSFILTER inside one measure would be safer
Treating a snowflaked dimension structure as fine, when it's the root cause enabling the ambiguity in the first place
keyPoints: Bidirectional relationships let a filter propagate in both directions between two tables
Ambiguity arises when multiple valid filter paths exist between the same two tables
Both can cause a blocking warning or, worse, silent double-counting
Scoping bidirectional behavior to one measure with CROSSFILTER is safer than a model-wide Both relationship

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the multi-path ambiguity root cause
Correctly explains the double-counting/warning symptom
Proposes a correct resolution (CROSSFILTER scoping or star schema)

questions.title: Diagnosing a Slow Power BI Report
questions.prompt: A Power BI report that used to load instantly now takes 15+ seconds per visual interaction, and the model has grown to several hundred million rows. Walk through how you'd diagnose the bottleneck and the main levers you'd consider to fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start with Performance Analyzer in Power BI Desktop, which breaks down each visual's render time into DAX query time, visual rendering time, and other overhead, immediately telling me whether the bottleneck is the DAX engine (VertiPaq, formula engine) or something else like a slow custom visual. If DAX query time dominates, I'd capture the actual query with 'Copy query' and run it through DAX Studio to see the server timings split between the storage engine (scanning VertiPaq's compressed columns) and the formula engine (row-by-row DAX evaluation, often the sign of a poorly written measure using iterators unnecessarily or triggering many small storage engine queries). At several hundred million rows, the most durable fix is usually pre-aggregating: building an aggregation table at a coarser grain that Power BI's automatic aggregations feature (or a manually managed composite model) can serve most visual interactions from, falling back to the full-detail table only when a user drills to a grain the aggregation doesn't cover. Other levers include reviewing whether DirectQuery is being used where Import or a hybrid composite model would perform far better, checking for inefficient measures (nested CALCULATE calls, iterators over the full fact table instead of a pre-filtered context), and confirming the model's star schema is clean, since excessive bidirectional relationships or a poorly structured snowflake can force the engine to do far more work than necessary per query.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is always Performance Analyzer, because it tells me immediately whether I'm looking at a DAX problem, a rendering problem, or something else entirely -- no point tuning measures if the real issue is a slow custom visual. If the time really is in the DAX query, I'd grab that query and drop it into DAX Studio to see the server timings breakdown -- storage engine time versus formula engine time specifically, because those point to very different fixes. A lot of formula engine time usually means a measure is doing row-by-row work it doesn't need to, often an iterator that should be a simple aggregation, or CALCULATE nested in a way that's generating many small queries instead of one efficient one. Given the scale here -- several hundred million rows -- I wouldn't expect tuning individual measures alone to get me back to instant; I'd seriously look at building aggregation tables at the grain most visuals actually need, and letting Power BI's automatic aggregations feature route most queries to that smaller table, only hitting the full fact table when someone genuinely drills down past what the aggregation covers. I'd also sanity-check the model shape itself -- if there's DirectQuery where Import would work, or bidirectional relationships that aren't actually needed, those are often cheaper, more durable fixes than trying to hand-tune every slow measure one at a time.
questions.example: A region-level dashboard querying a 400M-row fact table directly: adding an aggregation table pre-summarized by Region and Month, with automatic aggregations enabled, lets most visuals resolve from a few thousand rows instead of 400 million, only falling back to full detail when a user drills to the daily/transaction grain.
commonMistakes: Tuning DAX measures before confirming with Performance Analyzer that DAX query time is actually the bottleneck
Not distinguishing storage engine time from formula engine time when diagnosing a slow query in DAX Studio
Reaching for a Premium capacity upgrade as the first fix instead of first checking model design and aggregations
Leaving unnecessary bidirectional relationships or a snowflaked schema in place at large scale
keyPoints: Performance Analyzer isolates whether the bottleneck is DAX, rendering, or visuals
DAX Studio's server timings separate storage engine time from formula engine time
Aggregation tables are the most durable fix at hundreds of millions of rows
Model shape issues (DirectQuery misuse, unnecessary bidirectional relationships) compound performance problems at scale

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a logical diagnostic sequence starting with Performance Analyzer
Correctly explains the storage engine vs. formula engine distinction
Proposes aggregation tables as the main scale fix
Mentions model shape/design as a contributing factor

questions.title: Scheduled Refresh Failing Through an On-Premises Gateway
questions.prompt: A Power BI dataset's scheduled refresh has started failing intermittently with a gateway timeout, but manual refreshes from the Power BI service work fine. Walk through how you'd investigate this.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd start in the Power BI admin portal's gateway management area and check the gateway cluster's health and recent refresh history for the actual error detail, since 'timeout' can mean several different things -- a query genuinely taking too long against the source, the gateway machine running low on resources during the scheduled window, or a network path issue between the gateway and the source that's intermittent rather than constant. The fact that manual refreshes succeed but scheduled ones intermittently fail points toward something time-of-day or load-dependent: if the scheduled refresh runs at a time when other jobs are also hitting the same gateway machine or the same source database, resource contention on the gateway host (CPU, memory) or connection pool exhaustion on the source is a strong candidate, which I'd check against gateway machine performance counters and the source database's own activity logs for that time window. I'd also check whether the gateway cluster has more than one gateway installed for high availability and load balancing -- a single-gateway setup has no failover, so any transient issue on that one machine takes down every scheduled refresh routed through it. If the underlying queries are simply slow against a large source, increasing the dataset's query timeout settings or optimizing the Power Query steps (ensuring query folding is actually happening, so the heavy lifting runs at the source rather than through the gateway) is the longer-term fix.
questions.professionalAnswer: Since manual refreshes work and scheduled ones don't, the first thing I suspect is something that's different about the timing, not the query itself. I'd check the gateway's refresh history in the admin portal first for the actual error text behind 'timeout' -- that detail usually points at whether it's the source being slow, the gateway machine itself struggling, or a network blip. Because it's intermittent and specific to the scheduled window, I'd look hard at what else is running on that gateway machine or against that source at the same time -- if there's a batch job or another scheduled refresh competing for the same resources, that's a classic cause of exactly this symptom. I'd also check whether this is a single-gateway setup with no redundancy; if so, any transient hiccup on that one machine takes out every refresh scheduled through it, and setting up a gateway cluster with multiple members for load balancing and failover is often the real fix, not just a timeout tweak. If the queries themselves are genuinely heavy, I'd also double check that Power Query's steps are still folding back to the source -- an unfolded step means way more data crossing the gateway than necessary, which gets worse under any kind of resource pressure.
questions.example: The gateway's event logs show the scheduled refresh consistently failing at 2 AM, the same window a separate nightly ETL job runs against the same source database, pointing to resource contention rather than a dataset design problem.
commonMistakes: Assuming 'timeout' always means the same root cause without checking the actual gateway error detail
Not checking what else runs on the gateway machine or source database during the scheduled window
Running a single-gateway setup with no high-availability cluster for a business-critical refresh
Jumping straight to raising the query timeout setting without investigating why the query is slow in the first place
keyPoints: Gateway refresh history provides the specific error detail behind a generic timeout message
Intermittent, time-specific failures point toward resource contention during that window
A single-gateway setup has no failover, so any machine issue takes down all its scheduled refreshes
Confirming query folding is still happening reduces the data volume crossing the gateway

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes checking gateway refresh history for specific error detail
Correctly reasons about why manual succeeds but scheduled fails (timing/contention)
Mentions gateway cluster redundancy as a relevant consideration
Mentions query folding/optimization as a longer-term fix

questions.title: Tableau Fan-Out From a Join on a One-to-Many Relationship
questions.prompt: A Tableau workbook joins Orders to OrderLineItems, and the SUM of order-level TotalDue is showing numbers several times larger than expected. Explain why, and the two different ways you could fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: A join between Orders and OrderLineItems on OrderID produces one row per line item, not one row per order -- an order with five line items appears five times in the joined result, each copy carrying the same order-level TotalDue value. Any aggregation of TotalDue, like SUM, then adds that same value five times for that one order, inflating the total by a factor matching however many line items each order has (this is the classic 'fan-out' problem). The first fix is to use a Tableau data source relationship (the newer, default modeling approach since the 'Relationships' feature) instead of a physical join -- relationships preserve each table's native level of detail and perform aggregation at the appropriate grain before combining results, so an order-level measure like TotalDue is summed correctly without being duplicated per line item. The second fix, if a physical join is required for some reason, is to aggregate line-item-level measures before the join (via a derived table or custom SQL doing a pre-join GROUP BY), or to use a Level of Detail expression like { FIXED [OrderID] : MIN([TotalDue]) } on the order-level field to collapse the duplicated values back down to one value per order before summing.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is the textbook join fan-out problem, and the fix I reach for by default now is simply not using a physical join at all -- Tableau's relationships feature was built specifically to solve this. A join between Orders and OrderLineItems on OrderID literally duplicates every order-level column once per line item, so an order with five lines shows TotalDue five separate times, and SUM naively adds all five copies, inflating the real total fivefold. If I switch Orders and OrderLineItems to a relationship instead of a physical join, Tableau keeps each table at its own native grain and aggregates appropriately depending on which fields are actually in the view, so TotalDue gets summed correctly at the order grain without multiplying through the line-item duplication. If I'm stuck with a physical join for some legacy reason, my fallback is a LOD expression -- something like { FIXED [OrderID] : MIN([TotalDue]) } -- which collapses the duplicated order-level value back to one true value per order before I sum it, regardless of how many line-item rows are sitting behind it in the joined result.
questions.example: An order with TotalDue = $500 and 4 line items appears as 4 rows post-join, each showing $500; a naive SUM([TotalDue]) across those 4 rows returns $2,000 instead of the correct $500.
commonMistakes: Not recognizing join fan-out as the cause of an inflated SUM at the parent grain
Defaulting to a physical join out of habit instead of using Tableau's relationships feature
Using AVG as a band-aid instead of actually fixing the duplication at its root
Forgetting a LOD fix like FIXED/MIN still needs the correct dimension (OrderID) to collapse on
keyPoints: A one-to-many join duplicates parent-level values once per child row
SUM over the duplicated values inflates the result by the duplication factor
Tableau relationships avoid fan-out by preserving each table's native grain
A FIXED LOD expression can collapse duplicated values back to one per key when a physical join is unavoidable

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the fan-out mechanism causing the inflation
Correctly proposes relationships as the primary fix
Correctly proposes an LOD-based fallback fix for physical joins

questions.title: ADF Self-Hosted Integration Runtime Connectivity Failure
questions.prompt: A pipeline reading from an on-premises SQL Server through a self-hosted integration runtime (SHIR) started failing overnight with connection errors, though nothing in the pipeline itself changed. Walk through your troubleshooting steps.
questions.modelAnswer: Since the pipeline definition didn't change, I'd focus on the self-hosted IR's environment rather than the pipeline logic itself. First, I'd check the SHIR's status in the ADF portal (Manage > Integration Runtimes) -- if it shows as disconnected or the node status is unhealthy, that confirms the problem is on the runtime side, not ADF's orchestration. From there I'd check the actual SHIR machine: whether the Integration Runtime Windows service is still running, whether the machine rebooted (a Windows patch cycle is a common silent cause), and the local Diagnostics tab in the Integration Runtime Configuration Manager app on that machine, which tests connectivity to both the Azure Relay/Service Bus endpoint ADF uses to communicate with the SHIR and the on-prem data source itself. I'd also check whether a credential or password used in the linked service to connect to the on-prem SQL Server expired or rotated overnight, since that produces a connection error that looks infrastructure-related but is really a credential problem. Network-level causes to check include a firewall rule change, a VPN/ExpressRoute connectivity blip between the SHIR machine and Azure, or the on-prem SQL Server itself being unreachable due to its own maintenance window or restart.
questions.professionalAnswer: Nothing in the pipeline changing is actually useful information -- it tells me to stop looking at the pipeline JSON and start looking at the environment the SHIR lives in. My first stop is the Integration Runtimes page in ADF's Manage hub, checking whether the node shows connected or not; if it's disconnected, I already know the issue is on the runtime side. From there I'd remote into the actual SHIR machine and check a few things in order: is the Integration Runtime service even running, did the machine reboot overnight for a patch cycle, and what does the Diagnostics tab inside the Integration Runtime Configuration Manager say about connectivity to both Azure and the on-prem source. I'd also specifically check whether a password or service account used in the linked service happened to expire or rotate overnight -- that's a sneaky one because the error message often just says 'connection failed' without making it obvious it's actually an authentication problem, not a network one. And if none of that turns anything up, I'd widen the net to the network path itself -- a firewall change, VPN/ExpressRoute hiccup, or even the source SQL Server having its own overnight maintenance window that took it offline temporarily.
questions.example: The SHIR machine applied a Windows security update overnight that required a reboot; the Integration Runtime service didn't automatically restart afterward, leaving the node showing 'disconnected' in ADF and failing every pipeline routed through it until the service was manually restarted.
commonMistakes: Focusing on the pipeline definition when nothing there changed, instead of checking the SHIR environment
Not checking the SHIR node's connected/disconnected status in the ADF portal first
Overlooking an expired or rotated credential as the cause of a generic 'connection failed' error
Not checking whether the SHIR machine itself rebooted or lost its service state overnight
keyPoints: Check the SHIR node's connected status in ADF's Manage hub first
Verify the Integration Runtime service is running on the SHIR machine itself
Use the local Diagnostics tool to test connectivity to both Azure and the on-prem source
Rule out an expired/rotated credential, which can look like a network error

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly starts by checking SHIR node status rather than the pipeline
Describes checking the SHIR machine's service state and local diagnostics
Considers credential expiration as a plausible cause
Considers broader network/firewall causes

questions.title: Diagnosing and Rerunning a Failed ADF Pipeline
questions.prompt: An ADF pipeline with 20 activities failed at activity 14 overnight. Explain how you'd find the actual cause in the Monitor tab, and why 'Rerun from failed activity' is usually better than rerunning the whole pipeline.
questions.modelAnswer: In the Monitor tab's pipeline runs view, clicking into the specific failed run shows each activity's status as a visual graph, and clicking the failed activity itself (activity 14, shown in red) opens its Input/Output/Error details -- the Error tab typically has the actual exception message and error code from whatever that activity was doing (a copy activity's source/sink error, a stored procedure's SQL error, a data flow's transformation failure), which is the real diagnostic signal, not just 'activity failed.' I'd also check the Input and Output tabs to see exactly what parameters that activity run with, since a failure that only happens with specific parameter values (like a particular date range or file) points to a data problem rather than an infrastructure problem. Once the root cause is identified and fixed, 'Rerun from failed activity' resumes execution starting at activity 14 using the same pipeline run's parameters and the already-successful output of activities 1-13, rather than re-executing everything from the start -- this matters because activities 1-13 may have done meaningful, possibly non-idempotent work (like a data load that would duplicate if re-run) or simply be slow enough that re-running them unnecessarily wastes time and compute, especially overnight when a fast recovery matters.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd click into the specific failed pipeline run in Monitor, find activity 14 highlighted in red in the activity graph, and open its details -- the Error tab there is where the real information lives, whether that's a SQL error from a stored procedure activity, a copy activity complaining about a schema mismatch, or a data flow transformation error. I'd also check what parameters that specific run passed into activity 14, since a failure tied to one particular file or date range usually means a data issue upstream, not an ADF or infrastructure problem. Once I know what actually broke and fix it, I'd use Rerun from Failed Activity rather than rerunning the whole pipeline from scratch, for a pretty practical reason -- activities 1 through 13 already succeeded, and some of them might not be safe to run twice without creating duplicates, and even if they are safe, there's no reason to burn the time and compute re-doing work that already completed successfully overnight. Rerun from Failed Activity picks up exactly where it left off, using the same run's context, which gets the pipeline back to a healthy state the fastest.
questions.example: Activity 14's Error tab shows 'Violation of PRIMARY KEY constraint' from a stored procedure activity, pointing to a duplicate key in that night's source data rather than an ADF infrastructure issue; after cleaning the source row, Rerun from Failed Activity resumes at activity 14 without redoing activities 1-13.
commonMistakes: Rerunning the entire pipeline by default instead of checking whether failed activities can resume from where they stopped
Not opening the Error tab on the specific failed activity and guessing at the cause instead
Overlooking that some upstream activities might not be idempotent, making a full rerun risky, not just slow
Not checking the Input/parameters of the failed activity run, missing a data-specific root cause
keyPoints: The Monitor tab's activity graph highlights the specific failed activity
The Error tab on that activity has the actual exception detail, the real diagnostic signal
Checking Input/parameters helps distinguish a data-specific cause from an infrastructure cause
Rerun from Failed Activity resumes using prior successful output, avoiding redundant or unsafe re-execution

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes finding the failed activity and reading its Error detail
Correctly explains the benefit of Rerun from Failed Activity over a full rerun
Mentions idempotency/safety considerations for upstream activities

questions.title: Snowflake Query Suddenly Slower Despite No Data Growth
questions.prompt: A dashboard query against a 2 billion row Snowflake table that used to run in 3 seconds now takes 40 seconds, and the table's row count has barely changed. Walk through what you'd check, including clustering and caching.
questions.modelAnswer: With row count roughly stable, I'd first rule out the simplest explanation -- a cold cache. Snowflake's result cache serves an identical query instantly if nothing relevant changed, and the warehouse's local SSD cache speeds up repeated scans of the same micro-partitions; if the warehouse was suspended (AUTO_SUSPEND) and just resumed, or if a different warehouse size is now being used, that cache advantage is gone and the query pays the full scan cost again. If the query is genuinely slower on a warm, appropriately-sized warehouse, I'd check clustering health with SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION on the table -- if the query filters heavily on a column that isn't well-clustered (a high clustering depth), Snowflake has to scan many more micro-partitions than it should to find matching rows, and clustering quality degrades naturally over time as new data lands in insertion order rather than the originally clustered order, especially on a table receiving frequent updates or out-of-order inserts. I'd also check EXPLAIN/the query profile for a change in the actual execution plan -- a join order change, a new full table scan where a partition pruning scan used to happen, or a change in how many partitions are actually being scanned (the 'partitions scanned' vs. 'partitions total' metric in the query profile is the single most telling number for this kind of regression).
questions.professionalAnswer: Since the row count hasn't really grown, I wouldn't assume this is just 'more data, naturally slower' -- something changed. My first check is the boring one: is this actually a cold-cache situation, because the warehouse got suspended for being idle and just spun back up, or because the query result cache got invalidated by some unrelated change to the table. If it's genuinely slow on a warm warehouse, I'd pull up the query profile and look at partitions scanned versus partitions total -- that ratio tells me immediately whether Snowflake is pruning effectively or scanning way more of the table than it should for this filter. If pruning looks bad, I'd check SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION on whatever column the query filters on -- clustering quality naturally degrades over time on a table that gets frequent out-of-order inserts or updates, even without huge row count growth, because new micro-partitions aren't landing in the same sorted order the table was originally clustered in. Depending on what I find, the fix is either reclustering (automatic clustering, if a clustering key is defined, or manually re-clustering) or just confirming the warehouse size and cache state are what they used to be before assuming anything structural changed at all.
commonMistakes: Assuming the slowdown must be due to data growth without checking the actual row count change
Not checking cache state (result cache, warehouse warm cache) before investigating structural causes
Skipping the query profile's partitions-scanned metric, missing the clearest signal of a pruning regression
Not knowing clustering quality degrades over time independent of total row count growth
keyPoints: Cold cache (suspended warehouse, invalidated result cache) is the simplest explanation to rule out first
The query profile's partitions-scanned vs. partitions-total ratio reveals pruning effectiveness
SYSTEM$CLUSTERING_INFORMATION reveals clustering depth/quality on the filtered column
Clustering quality degrades over time from out-of-order inserts/updates, independent of total row growth

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Checks cache/warehouse state before structural causes
Correctly uses the query profile's partition pruning metric
Correctly checks clustering quality and explains its degradation over time

questions.title: A dbt Incremental Model Silently Missing Late-Arriving Rows
questions.prompt: A dbt incremental model using the default append strategy with a WHERE updated_at > max(updated_at) filter is missing rows that were updated a few hours ago but inserted into the source with a slight delay. Diagnose the cause and fix it.
questions.modelAnswer: The problem is a race condition between when a row's updated_at timestamp gets set and when that row actually becomes visible/committed in the source system that dbt's incremental query reads from. If a row is stamped with updated_at = 2:00 PM but doesn't actually land in the queryable source table until 2:05 PM due to replication lag or a slightly delayed write, and the dbt incremental run executes at 2:03 PM using MAX(updated_at) from the target as its cutoff, that run's filter boundary is set at a time before the late row was actually available -- the next run's filter, now based on a MAX(updated_at) that already includes everything up to 2:00 PM, will never go back and pick up that 2:00 PM-stamped row that only became visible at 2:05 PM, because the filter logically treats anything at or before the already-seen maximum as already processed. The standard fix is to build in a safety lookback window: instead of filtering strictly greater than the exact previous max, subtract a buffer (WHERE updated_at > (SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM {{ this }}) - INTERVAL '2 hours'), intentionally re-scanning a small overlap of recently processed time so a late-arriving row that was missed on an earlier run gets picked up on a later one, relying on the model's unique_key merge logic to safely re-process already-loaded rows as idempotent no-ops.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is a timing problem, not a logic bug in the filter itself -- the updated_at timestamp gets written slightly before the row is actually visible to a query against the source, so if dbt's incremental run happens to land in that gap, it computes its 'already processed up to here' watermark using a MAX(updated_at) that's technically correct for the data it saw, but the row that arrives a few minutes later with an earlier timestamp falls behind that watermark forever -- no future run's filter will go back far enough to catch it, because every future run assumes anything before the current max is already handled. I'd fix it with a deliberate overlap window: instead of filtering strictly greater than the previous max, I'd subtract a buffer, like two hours, so each run intentionally re-scans a bit of the recent past it already processed. That's safe specifically because the model has a unique_key and merges rather than blindly appending, so re-seeing an already-loaded row just results in a harmless re-update to the same values, not a duplicate. The buffer size is a judgment call based on how much lag the source realistically has -- I'd rather overlap more than strictly necessary than risk missing another late row.
commonMistakes: Filtering strictly on the exact previous max(updated_at) with no safety buffer
Not recognizing replication/write lag as the root cause of a late-arriving row being permanently missed
Assuming a wider buffer is risky, when it's safe as long as the model merges on a unique_key
Fixing this once but not periodically re-checking whether the source's actual lag has grown beyond the buffer size
keyPoints: The filter boundary is based on a watermark that assumes data visibility matches the timestamp, which isn't always true
A late-arriving row with an earlier timestamp can permanently fall behind the watermark
A deliberate lookback buffer subtracted from the max(updated_at) filter re-scans a safety window each run
This is safe specifically because a unique_key merge makes re-processing already-loaded rows idempotent

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the watermark/visibility race condition as the root cause
Correctly proposes a lookback buffer as the fix
Correctly explains why this fix is safe given the unique_key merge

questions.title: Fabric Capacity Throttling During a Heavy Refresh
questions.prompt: A shared Microsoft Fabric capacity starts rejecting or severely delaying interactive report queries every afternoon around the same time a large Lakehouse refresh job runs. Explain what's happening in terms of Fabric's capacity model, and the options for fixing it.
questions.modelAnswer: Fabric capacity is measured and billed in Capacity Units (CUs), shared across every workload running on that capacity -- Power BI reports, Lakehouse/Spark jobs, Data Factory pipelines, and so on all draw from the same pool. Fabric allows short-term bursting above the purchased CU level to absorb spikes, but it also uses smoothing, which spreads a job's actual CU consumption out over a rolling window rather than charging it all at the instant the job runs; a sustained heavy refresh can consume enough smoothed capacity that there's little headroom left for other workloads during and immediately after it, which is exactly why interactive report queries get delayed or throttled at a predictable time each day tied to that refresh. Once a capacity's utilization crosses certain thresholds, Fabric moves from bursting into throttling, where new requests get increasingly delayed and, if consumption stays high enough for long enough, eventually rejected outright. The fixes are: scheduling the heavy refresh for an off-peak window when interactive usage is lower, optimizing the refresh job itself to consume fewer CUs (more efficient Spark configuration, incremental refresh instead of a full reload), splitting workloads across separate capacities so a heavy batch job doesn't compete with interactive BI traffic on the same shared pool, or simply increasing the purchased capacity size (moving to a larger F-SKU) if the workload genuinely needs more headroom than the current capacity provides.
questions.professionalAnswer: This is capacity contention, plain and simple -- everything on a Fabric capacity, interactive Power BI queries included, draws from the same shared pool of Capacity Units, and Fabric's smoothing behavior means a heavy job doesn't just hit the capacity for a brief instant, it spreads its cost out over a rolling window, which can eat into the headroom available to other things running at the same time or shortly after. If the Lakehouse refresh is big enough, it can push the capacity into throttling territory during that window, which shows up to users as exactly what's described -- interactive reports getting slow or outright rejected, consistently around the same time every day the refresh runs. My first lever is almost always scheduling -- if I can move that refresh to a genuinely quiet window with little interactive usage, the contention mostly disappears without touching anything else. If that's not possible because the business needs fresher data during the day, I'd look at optimizing the refresh itself to use fewer capacity units, or separating workloads onto different capacities entirely so the batch job and the BI traffic aren't fighting over the same pool. If none of that's enough, the last lever is just buying more capacity, but I'd treat that as the expensive option to reach for only after the cheaper scheduling and optimization options are genuinely exhausted.
questions.example: A nightly Lakehouse transformation job that used to run at 2 AM gets rescheduled to 1 PM to meet a fresher-data requirement, and from that point forward, interactive report performance degrades every afternoon during the job's run -- moving it to a separate, dedicated capacity restores interactive performance without needing a bigger SKU.
commonMistakes: Assuming the report itself is the problem rather than capacity contention from a concurrent heavy job
Not understanding Fabric's smoothing behavior, which spreads CU consumption over a window rather than an instant
Jumping to buying a bigger capacity SKU before trying scheduling or workload separation
Running interactive BI workloads and heavy batch workloads on the same shared capacity without considering isolation
keyPoints: Fabric capacity is a shared pool of Capacity Units across all workload types
Smoothing spreads a job's CU consumption over a rolling window, affecting concurrent and nearby workloads
Sustained high utilization pushes the capacity from bursting into throttling
Fixes include rescheduling, optimizing the heavy job, workload isolation across capacities, or increasing capacity size

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains Fabric's shared capacity and smoothing model
Correctly connects the symptom to throttling from capacity contention
Proposes realistic, prioritized fixes

questions.title: The Small-File Problem in a Delta Table
questions.prompt: A streaming job writes micro-batches into a Delta table every minute, and after a few weeks, queries against the table have gotten noticeably slower even though total data volume hasn't grown unusually. Diagnose the cause and explain the fix, including its retention tradeoff.
questions.modelAnswer: A streaming job writing a small micro-batch every minute creates a large number of small Parquet files over time, since each write operation typically produces at least one new file per partition touched. Query performance degrades because the engine has to open and read metadata from a huge number of small files to answer a query, rather than a smaller number of well-sized files -- the per-file overhead (opening the file, reading its footer, planning around it) dominates when files are tiny, and this problem compounds the longer the streaming job runs without any compaction. The fix is running OPTIMIZE on the table periodically, which compacts many small files into a smaller number of larger, more efficient files (bin-packing), and pairing it with ZORDER BY on a column the queries commonly filter on, which co-locates related data within those compacted files so range-based filters can skip more data during a scan. The retention tradeoff shows up with the subsequent VACUUM step: OPTIMIZE doesn't delete the old small files immediately -- Delta keeps them around so that Time Travel queries against older table versions still have access to the files that made up that version -- so VACUUM is needed to actually reclaim storage by permanently deleting files no longer referenced by any version within the retention window, but running VACUUM with too short a retention period risks breaking a concurrent long-running query or a Time Travel query that's still relying on those older files, while too long a retention period leaves storage costs and clutter accumulating unnecessarily.
questions.professionalAnswer: A streaming job writing every minute is a classic recipe for the small-file problem -- each micro-batch commit tends to produce new, small files, and after a few weeks of that, the table can have an enormous number of tiny files even if the actual total data size isn't that large. Query performance suffers because reading a table with thousands of small files means paying file-open and metadata overhead thousands of times over, which adds up fast and has nothing to do with the real data volume. My fix is a scheduled OPTIMIZE job -- maybe nightly -- that bin-packs those small files into a sensible number of larger ones, and I'd pair it with ZORDER BY on whatever column the downstream queries filter on most, since that co-locates related rows together and makes range filters much more effective at skipping irrelevant data. The part people sometimes miss is that OPTIMIZE alone doesn't shrink storage costs, because the old small files stick around to support Time Travel against older versions of the table -- VACUUM is the step that actually deletes files no longer needed within the retention window. I'd be deliberate about that retention window too -- too short and I risk breaking a long-running query or a Time Travel use case that's still referencing an older file; too long and I'm paying for storage I don't need and letting file clutter build up for longer than necessary.
questions.example:
OPTIMIZE events_table ZORDER BY (event_date);
VACUUM events_table RETAIN 168 HOURS; -- keep 7 days of Time Travel history before reclaiming old files
commonMistakes: Not recognizing frequent small streaming writes as the cause of a growing small-file count
Running OPTIMIZE but forgetting VACUUM never runs, so storage costs keep growing despite compaction
Running VACUUM with an overly short retention period, breaking a running query or Time Travel use case
Choosing a ZORDER column that isn't actually used in common query filters, getting little benefit
keyPoints: Frequent small writes from streaming jobs accumulate into a large number of small files over time
OPTIMIZE bin-packs small files into fewer, larger, more query-efficient files
ZORDER BY co-locates related data to improve filter-based data skipping
VACUUM reclaims storage from old files, with a retention window tradeoff against Time Travel/long-running queries

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the small-file accumulation cause
Correctly describes OPTIMIZE and ZORDER as the fix
Correctly explains the VACUUM retention tradeoff

questions.title: Normalization vs. Star Schema Denormalization
questions.prompt: A new analyst asks why your data warehouse's dimension tables look so denormalized compared to the perfectly normalized OLTP system they came from. Explain the tradeoff and when you'd deliberately keep a dimension snowflaked instead.
questions.modelAnswer: A normalized OLTP schema minimizes redundancy and enforces data integrity by splitting related attributes into separate tables connected by foreign keys, which is exactly right for a system handling frequent, small, transactional writes where update anomalies need to be prevented. A star schema deliberately denormalizes dimension tables -- flattening what might be several related OLTP tables (Product, Category, Subcategory, Brand) into one wide DimProduct table -- because the warehouse's primary workload is read-heavy analytical queries, and every join a query has to perform adds cost and complexity; collapsing hierarchy levels into one dimension table means a report can filter or group by Category without an extra join, and the query optimizer has far fewer tables to reason about. The tradeoff is accepted redundancy (the category name is repeated on every product row in that category) and a need for a controlled ETL/ELT process to keep that denormalized data consistent, since there's no foreign-key-enforced single source of truth the way there is in a normalized schema. You'd deliberately keep a dimension snowflaked (partially normalized) when a sub-dimension is extremely large, changes at a very different frequency than the rest of the dimension, or is shared identically across many different dimensions, where the storage and update-maintenance savings of normalizing that one piece outweigh the extra join cost for queries that need it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them it's a deliberate tradeoff, not an oversight -- the OLTP system is optimized for exactly the opposite workload we're optimizing for in the warehouse.
