Normalization in OLTP exists to prevent update anomalies on a system doing lots of small, frequent writes; a star schema exists to make read-heavy analytical queries fast and simple, and the easiest way to do that is to flatten hierarchy levels that used to be separate tables into one wide dimension, so a report filtering by Category doesn't need an extra join to get there. The cost is redundancy -- the same category name sits on every product row in that category -- but we're trading storage and a controlled ETL process for dramatically simpler, faster queries, which is the right trade for a system where queries vastly outnumber writes. I'd still snowflake a piece of a dimension on purpose in specific cases -- if a sub-dimension is genuinely huge and shared identically across several parent dimensions, or updates on a totally different cadence than the rest of the dimension, normalizing just that piece can be worth the extra join, but that's the exception I reach for deliberately, not the default shape I design toward.
questions.example: DimProduct flattens ProductID, ProductName, CategoryName, SubcategoryName, and BrandName into one wide row per product, instead of requiring a query to join four separate normalized OLTP tables just to label one fact row by category.
commonMistakes: Treating a denormalized star schema as a modeling mistake rather than a deliberate performance tradeoff
Normalizing a warehouse dimension out of habit, adding unnecessary join cost to every analytical query
Not recognizing when a sub-dimension genuinely warrants snowflaking due to size or independent update cadence
Assuming denormalization means no process exists to keep the redundant data consistent
keyPoints: OLTP normalization optimizes for write integrity; star schema denormalization optimizes for read performance
Flattening hierarchy levels into a dimension reduces joins for common analytical queries
Redundancy is an accepted tradeoff, managed through a controlled ETL/ELT process
Snowflaking is reserved for cases where a sub-dimension's size or update cadence justifies the extra join cost

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the OLTP vs. warehouse workload tradeoff
Correctly explains the join-reduction benefit of denormalization
Gives a realistic case for deliberately snowflaking

questions.title: Choosing Import, DirectQuery, or a Composite Model
questions.prompt: A Power BI model needs to combine a slowly changing 50-million-row sales history with a near-real-time inventory feed that must reflect changes within seconds. Walk through how you'd decide between Import, DirectQuery, and a composite model.
questions.modelAnswer: Import would give the best query performance for the 50-million-row sales history since it loads into VertiPaq's compressed in-memory format, but it's the wrong choice for the inventory feed because a scheduled refresh can't realistically meet a near-real-time, within-seconds freshness requirement -- Import's freshness is bounded by how often you can practically refresh, typically minutes at best, not seconds. DirectQuery would satisfy the inventory feed's freshness requirement perfectly since every query goes live to the source, but applying DirectQuery to the full 50-million-row sales history would make every report interaction pay a live query cost against that large table, which is a poor tradeoff when that data barely changes. A composite model resolves this directly: put the sales history in Import mode and the inventory data in DirectQuery mode within the same model, which Power BI explicitly supports by design -- each table gets the storage mode appropriate to its actual freshness and performance needs, and relationships between an Import table and a DirectQuery table work correctly as long as the model is aware it's operating across storage modes (and any such table touched by a DirectQuery relationship effectively behaves as 'Dual' or limited mode for certain calculations). This is exactly the scenario composite models were designed for: mixed freshness requirements within one report.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split this decision by what each piece of data actually needs. The sales history barely changes and is huge, so Import is the obvious fit there -- it loads into VertiPaq's compressed format and gives the best possible query performance, and a scheduled refresh every hour or even daily is perfectly fine for data that's basically static. The inventory feed is the opposite: it needs to reflect changes within seconds, and there's no refresh schedule that gets Import there -- that's squarely a DirectQuery requirement, where every query goes straight to the live source. Trying to force one storage mode across both would mean either DirectQuery slowing down every interaction with the 50-million-row sales history for no real freshness benefit, or Import making the inventory numbers stale in a way that defeats the entire point of showing them. A composite model is built for exactly this situation -- I'd set sales history to Import and inventory to DirectQuery in the same model, and Power BI handles relationships across the two storage modes correctly, as long as I'm aware that any table touched by a DirectQuery relationship picks up some of DirectQuery's behavior for certain calculations, which is a detail worth testing carefully before calling the model done.
questions.example: A composite model: DimProduct and FactSalesHistory in Import mode, FactInventory in DirectQuery mode against the live inventory system, joined to the same DimProduct, giving fast historical analysis and live inventory numbers in one report.
commonMistakes: Forcing one storage mode across the whole model instead of matching mode to each table's actual freshness need
Assuming DirectQuery on the large, rarely-changing table is a reasonable tradeoff for simplicity
Not testing how Dual/limited-relationship behavior affects calculations once a composite model is in place
Underestimating the refresh frequency a near-real-time requirement actually needs before ruling out Import
keyPoints: Import gives the best performance but is bounded by refresh frequency, unsuitable for seconds-level freshness
DirectQuery meets live freshness needs but adds per-query latency, unsuitable for a large, mostly static table
A composite model lets different tables use different storage modes within one model
Relationships across storage modes introduce Dual/limited behavior worth testing explicitly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly reasons about Import's unsuitability for the inventory feed
Correctly reasons about DirectQuery's unsuitability for the full sales history
Correctly recommends and explains a composite model

questions.title: Tableau Extracts vs. Live Connections
questions.prompt: A Tableau Server dashboard connected live to a data warehouse is slow under concurrent load during business hours, but the warehouse team doesn't want hundreds of dashboard users hitting their cluster directly. Explain the tradeoffs of switching to an extract, and how you'd handle freshness.
questions.modelAnswer: A live connection sends a native query to the source for every interaction, which means query performance and concurrency load scale directly with however many users are clicking around the dashboard at once -- hundreds of concurrent users each triggering their own warehouse queries is exactly the load pattern that stresses a shared cluster and produces the slowness described. An extract (Hyper) pre-pulls and stores a compressed, columnar copy of the data on Tableau Server's own infrastructure, so once it's built, every subsequent dashboard interaction queries that local Hyper file instead of the source warehouse at all -- concurrency load shifts entirely off the warehouse and onto Tableau Server's extract engine, which is specifically built to handle many concurrent analytical queries efficiently. The tradeoff is freshness: an extract is only as current as its last refresh, so the business has to accept some amount of staleness, typically managed with a scheduled extract refresh (hourly, nightly, or more frequent incremental refreshes that only pull new/changed rows rather than rebuilding the whole extract). The right freshness cadence depends on how time-sensitive the dashboard's decisions actually are -- a daily sales summary dashboard tolerates a nightly refresh fine, while a dashboard genuinely needing intraday updates would need incremental refreshes scheduled more frequently, which is a real engineering and scheduling cost worth discussing with the business before committing to it.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain this as moving the query load off the warehouse and onto Tableau's own infrastructure instead. Right now, every one of those hundreds of concurrent users is sending a live query straight to the warehouse cluster, which is exactly the load pattern that's going to stress a shared resource, especially during business hours when everyone's looking at the same dashboard at once. Switching to an extract means Tableau Server pulls and stores a compressed copy of the data once, on a schedule, and every dashboard interaction after that queries the local Hyper extract instead of the warehouse at all -- which is a much better fit for high-concurrency interactive use, since Hyper's built specifically for that pattern. The honest tradeoff I'd walk the business through is freshness: the dashboard is now only as current as the last extract refresh, so I'd ask how time-sensitive the decisions being made off this dashboard really are. If daily is fine, a nightly full refresh works. If they genuinely need intraday numbers, I'd set up an incremental refresh that only pulls new or changed rows on a more frequent schedule, instead of rebuilding the whole extract from scratch every time, which keeps the warehouse load low even with more frequent refreshes.
questions.example: A sales dashboard switches from a live connection to a nightly full extract refresh plus an hourly incremental refresh pulling only same-day new orders, keeping concurrency load off the warehouse while still reflecting same-day activity within the hour.
commonMistakes: Assuming extracts always mean 'stale until tomorrow' without considering incremental refresh schedules
Not discussing the actual freshness requirement with the business before choosing a refresh cadence
Switching to a live connection by default for 'accuracy' without weighing the concurrency cost on the source
Forgetting an incremental refresh needs a reliable column (like an updated timestamp) to identify new/changed rows
keyPoints: A live connection's query load scales directly with concurrent dashboard users against the source
An extract shifts query load onto Tableau Server's Hyper engine, built for concurrent analytical queries
The tradeoff is freshness, managed through a scheduled full or incremental refresh
Incremental refreshes reduce warehouse load even at a more frequent refresh cadence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the concurrency load shift from live to extract
Correctly articulates the freshness tradeoff
Proposes a reasonable refresh cadence/incremental strategy

questions.title: Sizing and Scaling Snowflake Virtual Warehouses
questions.prompt: A single Medium-sized Snowflake warehouse serves both a nightly batch ETL load and ad hoc BI queries during the day, and both are suffering: the ETL load is slow and BI queries queue up behind it during business hours. Propose an architecture that fixes both without just buying a bigger warehouse blindly.
questions.modelAnswer: The core problem is two workloads with very different characteristics sharing one compute resource: ETL benefits from raw compute size for a bounded period (bigger warehouse = faster single job, scaling vertically), while interactive BI benefits from concurrency handling across many simultaneous small queries (which Snowflake handles via multi-cluster warehouses scaling horizontally, not just a bigger single warehouse). Running both on one Medium warehouse means the ETL job's heavy resource usage directly competes with and queues behind (or in front of) BI queries, since they're sharing the same single compute cluster's query queue. The fix is separating them into dedicated virtual warehouses: a warehouse sized appropriately for the ETL job's workload (possibly a Large or X-Large run only during its batch window, auto-suspended immediately after), and a separate, smaller multi-cluster warehouse dedicated to BI traffic, configured to auto-scale out additional clusters when concurrent query volume increases during business hours, rather than queuing. Because Snowflake bills by warehouse-second of actual compute used, this separation doesn't necessarily cost more overall -- it just allocates spend to where each workload actually needs it, and critically, each workload no longer blocks or slows the other, since they're running on physically separate compute.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd stop thinking of this as 'one warehouse that's too small' and start thinking of it as two workloads that shouldn't be sharing a warehouse at all. ETL and interactive BI have fundamentally different resource needs -- ETL wants a burst of raw compute for a bounded window, which is a vertical scaling problem (bump the warehouse size up during the batch window, then suspend it), while BI wants to handle a lot of concurrent small queries without queuing, which is a horizontal scaling problem that Snowflake solves with multi-cluster warehouses, not just a bigger single warehouse. Right now both are stuck sharing one compute cluster's queue, so the ETL job and the BI traffic are directly competing for the same resource at exactly the time both need to run. My proposal is to split them: give the ETL job its own appropriately-sized warehouse that only runs during its batch window and auto-suspends immediately after, and give BI its own separate, smaller multi-cluster warehouse that scales out additional clusters automatically as concurrent query volume rises during the day. Since Snowflake bills by actual compute-second used, this isn't automatically more expensive -- it's just spending compute where each workload actually needs it, and the real win is that neither workload is blocking the other anymore because they're not sharing a queue at all.
questions.example: ETL_WH (Large, auto-suspend 60s) runs the nightly batch load in isolation; BI_WH (Small, multi-cluster, min 1/max 4 clusters, auto-scale) serves daytime dashboard traffic, scaling out additional clusters automatically as concurrent users increase, with neither warehouse ever queuing behind the other.
commonMistakes: Assuming the fix is simply a bigger single warehouse for everything, without separating workload types
Not distinguishing vertical scaling (warehouse size, good for a single heavy job) from horizontal scaling (multi-cluster, good for concurrency)
Leaving the ETL warehouse running (not auto-suspending) outside its batch window, wasting spend
Underestimating that cost can stay flat or even drop when compute is allocated to the right workload instead of oversized everywhere
keyPoints: ETL and interactive BI have different resource profiles: vertical scaling for ETL, horizontal/concurrency scaling for BI
Sharing one warehouse makes the two workloads compete for the same compute queue
Dedicated, appropriately-scoped warehouses per workload remove that contention
Multi-cluster warehouses auto-scale for BI concurrency; auto-suspend controls ETL warehouse cost outside its batch window

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses workload contention as the root cause
Correctly distinguishes vertical scaling (ETL) from horizontal/multi-cluster scaling (BI)
Proposes a concrete dedicated-warehouse architecture with cost controls

questions.title: Choosing dbt Materializations Across a Project
questions.prompt: Explain how you'd decide between view, table, incremental, and ephemeral materializations for different layers of a staging/intermediate/marts dbt project, and the main risk of over-using ephemeral models.
questions.modelAnswer: At the staging layer, where models mostly do light renaming/casting/cleanup directly on top of raw sources, view materialization is usually the right default -- there's little computation to save by persisting the result, and a view guarantees staging always reflects the current state of the source without a separate refresh step. Intermediate models, which often combine or reshape multiple staging models with real computation (joins, aggregations, window functions), benefit from being either views if lightweight, or tables if the computation is expensive enough that recomputing it as part of every downstream query would be wasteful. Mart-layer fact and dimension tables, which get queried repeatedly by BI tools and need to perform well, should almost always be table or incremental materializations -- incremental specifically for large fact tables where a full rebuild on every run would be unnecessarily slow, since incremental only processes new or changed rows on subsequent runs. Ephemeral materialization inlines a model's SQL directly into whatever references it, as a CTE, with no database object created at all -- useful for a small, simple transformation step that exists mainly for logical organization and is only referenced once or twice. The main risk of overusing ephemeral models is that inlining them as CTEs means the same underlying logic gets recomputed every single time it's referenced (no materialized, reusable result exists anywhere), and heavily nested ephemeral models can produce enormous, hard-to-read, hard-to-debug compiled SQL once dbt actually inlines several layers of CTEs into the final query sent to the warehouse.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd generally map materialization to how expensive the transformation is and how often it gets reused. Staging models are almost always views for me -- they're light renaming and casting, there's nothing expensive to save by persisting them, and keeping them as views means they always reflect the current source without needing their own refresh. Intermediate models depend on what they're actually doing -- if it's a real join or aggregation that downstream models would otherwise recompute over and over, I'll materialize it as a table. Marts are where performance really matters because BI tools query them repeatedly, so those are tables, or incremental specifically for large fact tables where rebuilding the whole thing every run would be wasteful and slow. Ephemeral is the one I use sparingly and deliberately -- it's great for a small logical step I want to name for readability but don't actually need as its own object, since dbt just inlines it as a CTE wherever it's referenced. The risk is exactly that inlining: if I chain several ephemeral models together, or reference the same ephemeral model from multiple places, that same logic gets recomputed every time instead of being computed once and reused, and the final compiled SQL can turn into a genuinely hard-to-read wall of nested CTEs that's painful to debug when something goes wrong.
questions.example: stg_orders (view) -> int_orders_joined_customers (table, real join + aggregation) -> fct_orders (incremental, large fact table) -> dim_customers (table, BI-facing dimension); a small ephemeral helper model used once inside int_orders_joined_customers for readability, not reused elsewhere.
commonMistakes: Materializing every staging model as a table out of habit, adding unnecessary storage and refresh overhead
Using ephemeral for a model referenced in multiple downstream models, causing repeated recomputation
Not using incremental for a genuinely large fact table, paying for an unnecessary full rebuild every run
Chaining many ephemeral models together, producing an unreadable, hard-to-debug compiled SQL statement
keyPoints: Staging models default to view since there's little expensive computation to persist
Intermediate models become tables when they perform real, reusable computation
Mart-layer tables use table or incremental materialization based on data volume and refresh needs
Ephemeral models inline as CTEs, risking repeated recomputation and unreadable compiled SQL if overused

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly maps each project layer to an appropriate materialization
Correctly explains ephemeral's CTE-inlining behavior
Correctly identifies the recomputation/readability risk of overusing ephemeral

questions.title: OneLake Shortcuts vs. Copying Data Between Fabric Workspaces
questions.prompt: Two teams in different Fabric workspaces both need access to the same Lakehouse data, currently maintained by copying a nightly export between workspaces. Explain how a OneLake shortcut would change this architecture, and one real limitation to be aware of.
questions.modelAnswer: A OneLake shortcut is a reference, not a copy -- it creates a pointer inside one Lakehouse (or workspace) to data that physically lives in another Lakehouse, another Fabric item, or even an external location like ADLS Gen2 or Amazon S3, and queries against the shortcut read the underlying data directly where it actually lives, with no duplication and no separate sync job needed. Replacing a nightly copy job with a shortcut means the second team's workspace always sees the current state of the source data instantly, not a snapshot that's up to a day stale, and it eliminates the storage cost of maintaining a duplicate copy along with the operational burden of monitoring and fixing a copy pipeline that can fail silently. The real limitation to flag is that a shortcut only addresses data access -- it does not duplicate or manage permissions automatically the same way a physically separate copy with its own independent access control might; access to the data through a shortcut is still governed by the underlying item's security model, so granting broader access via a shortcut requires actually managing permissions correctly on the source item, which needs careful planning in a multi-team setup where not every team should see everything in the source Lakehouse.
questions.professionalAnswer: A shortcut basically replaces 'copy the data every night' with 'point directly at where the data already lives.' Instead of a nightly export job moving data between workspaces, I'd set up a OneLake shortcut in the second team's Lakehouse that references the first team's Lakehouse data directly -- it's a reference, not a duplicate, so any query against it is reading the live, current data with zero lag and no separate storage cost for a second copy. That gets rid of the whole nightly copy pipeline, which is one less thing that can silently fail and leave one team working off stale data without realizing it. The limitation I'd flag before rolling this out broadly is around permissions -- a shortcut doesn't come with its own independent access control layer; whoever can query through the shortcut is still ultimately subject to the underlying source item's security model, so if the source Lakehouse has data that shouldn't be visible to every team using the shortcut, that needs to be solved with proper permission scoping on the source side, not assumed to be handled automatically just because it's 'only a shortcut.'
questions.example: Team B's Lakehouse gets a OneLake shortcut pointing at Team A's Lakehouse Sales table; Team B's queries read Team A's live data with no copy job, but Team B also implicitly needs appropriate read permission on Team A's underlying item for the shortcut to actually resolve.
commonMistakes: Describing a shortcut as a data copy rather than a live reference to data stored elsewhere
Assuming a shortcut solves permissions automatically, rather than inheriting the source item's security model
Not considering that removing the nightly copy job also removes the staleness buffer some downstream process might have relied on
Forgetting shortcuts can also point to external storage (ADLS Gen2, S3), not just other Fabric items
keyPoints: A OneLake shortcut is a reference to data stored elsewhere, not a physical copy
Shortcuts eliminate duplication, staleness, and the operational burden of a copy pipeline
Queries through a shortcut read the live underlying data directly
Access through a shortcut is still governed by the source item's own security model, requiring careful permission planning

questions.title: Fabric Lakehouse vs. Warehouse for a New Project
questions.prompt: A new Fabric project needs to support both data scientists writing PySpark notebooks against raw and curated data, and finance analysts who want a familiar T-SQL querying experience with strong transactional guarantees on the curated layer. Decide how you'd use Lakehouse and Warehouse items together.
questions.modelAnswer: A Fabric Lakehouse stores data as Delta tables on OneLake and is the natural fit for the data scientists' workload -- it supports Spark notebooks directly, handles both structured and unstructured data, and is where exploratory and transformation work on raw/curated data most naturally happens, read/written through Spark APIs with full Delta Lake semantics. A Fabric Warehouse provides a full T-SQL experience with stronger transactional (multi-table, multi-statement) guarantees than a Lakehouse's SQL endpoint offers, and is built for exactly the kind of structured, governed, T-SQL-first analytical querying the finance team wants. Rather than forcing one team onto the other's preferred tool, a common architecture uses a Lakehouse for the raw/bronze and curated/silver layers where Spark-based transformation happens, and a Warehouse for the gold/curated-for-consumption layer the finance team queries, populated from the Lakehouse (directly cross-querying Lakehouse tables from the Warehouse, or via a pipeline/notebook that writes curated results into Warehouse tables). Both items sit on the same OneLake storage underneath, so this isn't really data duplication in the traditional sense -- it's choosing the right compute/query engine on top of a shared storage layer for each team's actual workload and tooling preference.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't force either team onto the other's tool here -- I'd use both items for what each is actually good at. The data scientists want Spark notebooks and flexibility across raw and curated data, which is exactly what a Lakehouse gives them, since it's Delta tables on OneLake with full Spark read/write support. The finance team wants a T-SQL experience with real transactional guarantees, which is what a Warehouse is built for -- stronger multi-statement transaction support than querying a Lakehouse's SQL endpoint directly provides. My architecture would be: raw and curated transformation work happens in the Lakehouse where the data science team lives day to day, and then a governed, finance-facing gold layer gets built as Warehouse tables, populated from the Lakehouse's curated output, either through direct cross-querying between the two items or a scheduled pipeline that lands the finalized data into the Warehouse. Because both items ultimately sit on the same OneLake storage, this isn't the old pattern of fully duplicating data into two separate systems -- it's picking the right engine on top of shared storage for each team's actual workflow and SQL experience needs.
questions.example: Bronze/silver Delta tables in a Lakehouse, transformed via PySpark notebooks by the data science team; a nightly pipeline promotes the finalized gold-layer tables into a Warehouse item, where finance analysts run T-SQL queries with full transactional guarantees against a stable, governed schema.
commonMistakes: Forcing one team onto a tool that doesn't fit their actual workflow (SQL analysts into Spark notebooks, or vice versa)
Assuming Lakehouse and Warehouse require fully duplicating data rather than sharing OneLake storage
Not considering the stronger transactional guarantees a Warehouse offers over a Lakehouse SQL endpoint for the finance use case
Skipping a clear promotion path from curated Lakehouse data into the Warehouse's gold layer
keyPoints: Lakehouse fits Spark-based, flexible exploration and transformation on Delta tables
Warehouse fits T-SQL-first querying with stronger transactional guarantees
Both items can share the same underlying OneLake storage, avoiding full data duplication
A common pattern uses Lakehouse for raw/curated layers and Warehouse for the governed consumption layer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly matches each team's workload to the right item type
Proposes a coherent combined architecture
Correctly notes the shared OneLake storage avoiding full duplication

questions.title: Assigning Responsibilities Across a Medallion Architecture
questions.prompt: Design the bronze, silver, and gold layer responsibilities for a new Databricks medallion architecture ingesting raw e-commerce clickstream and order data, being specific about what transformation and quality work happens at each layer and why it shouldn't happen earlier or later.
questions.modelAnswer: Bronze holds raw, largely unmodified data exactly as it arrived from the source -- clickstream events and order records land here with minimal transformation (maybe basic type casting and adding ingestion metadata like load timestamp and source file name), and critically, bad or malformed records are not dropped at this layer; the goal is a faithful, replayable record of exactly what was received, so that any downstream problem can be traced back and reprocessed from a true original if a transformation bug is later discovered. Silver applies cleaning, deduplication, conformance to a consistent schema, and business-rule validation -- this is where malformed clickstream events get filtered out or flagged, where order records get joined with reference/dimension data for enrichment, and where the data starts looking like a structured, trustworthy, queryable table rather than a raw dump, but it's still generally organized close to the source system's natural grain rather than reshaped specifically for one business question. Gold is where data gets aggregated and modeled specifically for consumption -- dimensional models (fact/dimension tables) or pre-aggregated summary tables built for the specific reporting and analytics use cases the business actually needs, like a daily conversion funnel table joining clickstream sessions to orders. Doing quality/business-rule validation at bronze would be a mistake because it risks silently dropping or altering data you might need to reprocess later if the validation logic itself turns out to be wrong; doing it only at gold would be too late, because every downstream consumer of silver would inherit the same data quality problems repeatedly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep bronze as close to a faithful copy of what arrived as possible -- raw clickstream events and order records land there with maybe a type cast and some ingestion metadata, but nothing gets filtered out or 'fixed' yet, because I want a true record I can always go back to if I later discover a bug in how I was cleaning the data. Silver is where the real quality work happens -- deduplication, schema conformance, filtering out genuinely malformed events, joining orders against reference data for enrichment -- this is the layer where I'd actually trust the data enough to call it clean, but it's still shaped close to the source's natural structure, not yet reshaped around one specific business question. Gold is where I build for actual consumption -- a conversion funnel table joining clickstream sessions to the orders they led to, or whatever dimensional model the BI team actually queries against. The reason I wouldn't push validation earlier, into bronze, is that dropping bad data too early means I can't always get it back if my validation logic turns out to have a bug of its own -- I want to fix my logic and reprocess from a clean, complete bronze layer, not discover I already threw away the evidence. And I wouldn't push it later, to gold, because every table and every consumer sitting on top of silver would inherit the same unresolved quality issues over and over, instead of getting fixed once in the shared silver layer.
questions.example: A malformed clickstream event with a null session_id lands untouched in bronze; gets filtered out (or flagged in a quarantine table) during the silver transformation; and never appears at all in the gold-layer conversion funnel table, which only ever sees clean, validated silver data.
commonMistakes: Dropping or filtering bad records at bronze, losing the ability to reprocess from a true raw source later
Pushing all quality and business-rule validation to gold, letting every silver consumer inherit the same unresolved issues
Reshaping data specifically for one report's needs at the silver layer instead of keeping it close to the source grain
Not adding ingestion metadata (load timestamp, source file) at bronze, making later troubleshooting harder
keyPoints: Bronze preserves a faithful, unmodified, replayable copy of raw incoming data
Silver applies cleaning, deduplication, schema conformance, and business-rule validation once, for all downstream consumers
Gold models and aggregates data specifically for business consumption and reporting use cases
Validation belongs in silver, not bronze (loses reprocessing ability) or gold (lets issues propagate to every consumer)

deepDive.heading: Quarantine Tables for Rejected Silver Records
deepDive.content: Rather than silently dropping records that fail silver-layer validation, a more mature pattern routes them to a parallel quarantine table with the specific validation rule that failed attached as metadata. This lets a data engineer periodically review what's being rejected, catch validation rules that are too strict or genuinely buggy, and reprocess quarantined records once the underlying issue -- in the data or in the validation logic itself -- is resolved, rather than losing that data permanently.

deepDive.heading: Why Bronze Should Still Be Partitioned Thoughtfully
deepDive.content: Even though bronze avoids business-logic transformation, it still benefits from physical partitioning (commonly by ingestion date) and basic Delta table hygiene like periodic OPTIMIZE, since a 'just land everything raw' layer can otherwise become a performance bottleneck for the silver transformation jobs that read from it daily, especially once volume grows into the billions of rows typical of clickstream data.

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly assigns bronze's raw, unmodified responsibility
Correctly assigns silver's cleaning/validation/conformance responsibility
Correctly assigns gold's consumption-modeling responsibility
Correctly explains why validation belongs specifically at silver

questions.title: Choosing Fact Table Grain and Partitioning Strategy
questions.prompt: You're designing a fact table for order line items that will hold tens of billions of rows over its lifetime in Databricks. Explain how you'd decide the fact's grain, and how you'd choose a partitioning column, including a partitioning mistake that would hurt rather than help.
questions.modelAnswer: Grain is the single most important decision in fact table design: it defines exactly what one row represents, and every measure and dimension reference in the table must be true at that exact grain, with no mixing of levels. For order line items, the natural grain is one row per order line (not one row per order, which would force awkward aggregation of quantities and prices that actually vary per line), since that's the lowest level of detail the business actually needs to analyze -- which specific product, at which price, in which quantity, within which order. Once grain is fixed, partitioning should be chosen based on how the table is actually queried and loaded, not on an arbitrary high-cardinality column -- a date column (like order_date, typically at month or day granularity depending on query patterns and total volume) is the standard choice for a large fact table, because most analytical queries filter by a date range, and most loads append new data for a specific recent date, so partition pruning benefits both query performance and incremental load efficiency simultaneously. The partitioning mistake that hurts rather than helps is over-partitioning on a high-cardinality column, like partitioning by individual CustomerID or by day when day-level granularity produces too many small partitions relative to the data volume per partition -- this creates the small-file problem at the partition level, where the overhead of managing and pruning across a huge number of tiny partitions outweighs any filtering benefit, and can actually make queries slower than a more coarsely partitioned (or Z-ordered, unpartitioned) table would be.
questions.professionalAnswer: Grain comes first, always -- I'd fix it as one row per order line item, because that's the most granular level the business genuinely needs, and anything coarser, like one row per order, would force me to either lose line-level detail or awkwardly cram arrays of line items into a single row, which breaks standard dimensional modeling and makes simple aggregate queries unnecessarily complicated. Once the grain's locked, partitioning is a question about actual query and load patterns, not about picking whatever column has the most distinct values. For a fact table this size, I'd partition by order_date, usually at month granularity unless query patterns and daily volume specifically justify day-level partitions, because most analytical queries filter by a date range and most loads are appending recent data, so partition pruning helps both reads and writes. The mistake I'd specifically warn against is partitioning too finely relative to the actual data volume per partition -- partitioning by CustomerID, or by day when daily volume doesn't justify it, creates a huge number of small partitions, which turns into the exact same small-file problem that hurts performance rather than helping it, because now the engine's spending more effort managing and pruning across thousands of tiny partitions than it would have spent just scanning a more sensibly-sized, coarser partition layout.
questions.example: fct_order_line_items partitioned by order_date (month granularity): a report filtering WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-31' prunes to exactly one partition instead of scanning the full tens-of-billions-of-row table.
commonMistakes: Choosing a fact table grain coarser than what the business actually needs, losing analytical flexibility
Partitioning on a high-cardinality column like CustomerID instead of a query-aligned column like date
Over-partitioning (too fine a date granularity relative to data volume), recreating the small-file problem at the partition level
Choosing a partitioning column that doesn't match the table's actual filter or load patterns
keyPoints: Grain defines exactly what one fact row represents and must be consistent across every measure
Order line item is the correct grain here, avoiding forced aggregation of line-level detail
Partitioning should align with actual query filter patterns and load patterns, typically a date column
Over-partitioning on a high-cardinality or overly fine column recreates the small-file problem and hurts performance

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies and justifies the fact table's grain
Correctly proposes a query/load-aligned partitioning strategy
Correctly identifies an over-partitioning mistake and its consequence

questions.title: Disagreeing With a Stakeholder's Metric Definition
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time a stakeholder asked for a metric to be defined in a way you believed was technically misleading or inconsistent with how the business used it elsewhere. How did you handle the disagreement?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer names a specific, realistic disagreement -- for example, a stakeholder wanting 'active customer' to count anyone who logged in during the period, while every other report in the company defines it as someone who placed an order, which would make this one dashboard's numbers systematically incomparable to every other report using the term. The candidate should describe raising the concern directly but respectfully, grounding it in the business consequence rather than just technical correctness -- explaining specifically how the inconsistency would mislead decisions (two reports both claiming to show 'active customers' with very different numbers, with no one realizing why), not just asserting 'that's not how I'd define it.' A good resolution shows either successfully persuading the stakeholder to align with the existing definition, or, if the stakeholder had a genuinely valid reason for a different definition specific to their use case, proposing a clearly and differently named metric (like 'logged-in users' instead of overloading 'active customers') so both numbers can coexist without creating confusion. The answer should end with the actual outcome and ideally a concrete step taken afterward, like documenting the agreed definition somewhere the next person asking the same question could find it.
questions.professionalAnswer: This came up when a sales stakeholder wanted a dashboard to define 'active customer' as anyone who'd logged into the portal that month, but our finance and marketing reports had always defined it as someone who'd actually placed an order -- a much stricter bar. If I'd just built what was asked, we'd have had two dashboards both calling something 'active customers' with meaningfully different numbers, and no obvious way for a leader skimming both reports to know why. I raised it directly with the stakeholder, but I tried to frame it around the actual business risk rather than just 'that's inconsistent' -- I walked through what would happen the first time someone in a leadership meeting pulled up both numbers side by side and got confused about which was right. They actually had a legitimate reason to care about login activity specifically, so instead of forcing them into the existing definition, I suggested we keep 'active customer' meaning what it always meant everywhere else, and added a clearly separate metric called 'engaged users' for the login-based number they actually wanted. We documented both definitions in our metrics glossary afterward so the next person asking for 'active customers' wouldn't run into the same ambiguity.
commonMistakes: Giving a vague, non-specific answer with no real metric or stakeholder disagreement described
Framing the disagreement as purely about being technically correct rather than the business consequence
Describing capitulating immediately with no attempt to raise the concern at all
Describing digging in and refusing any compromise even when the stakeholder had a legitimate underlying need
keyPoints: Names a specific, realistic metric disagreement
Frames the concern around business consequences, not just technical correctness
Shows a genuine attempt to resolve the disagreement collaboratively, not just comply or dig in
Describes a concrete resolution and a follow-up action like documentation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a specific, credible scenario
Frames the disagreement around business impact
Shows a constructive, collaborative resolution approach
Describes a concrete outcome and follow-up

questions.title: Catching a Data Quality Issue Before It Reached Leadership
questions.prompt: Describe a time you caught a data quality issue in a report or pipeline shortly before it would have reached leadership or a key decision. What tipped you off, and what did you do?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer describes a specific detection method, not just 'I noticed something was off' -- for example, a routine sanity check comparing this week's revenue total against the prior week's, or a reconciliation between two systems that should match, revealing a number that jumped or dropped in a way that didn't match any known business event. The candidate should explain the actual investigation that found the root cause (a duplicate join introduced by a recent pipeline change, a currency conversion applied twice, a Snowflake incremental model missing a dedup step after an upstream schema change) rather than just saying 'I fixed it.' Critically, the answer should describe the communication that followed: proactively flagging the issue to whoever was about to present or act on the number, being transparent about what was wrong and what the corrected number actually was, rather than quietly patching it and hoping no one noticed the delay or the discrepancy. A strong answer also mentions what changed afterward to catch this category of issue earlier next time -- a new automated check, a reconciliation step added to the pipeline, or a sign-off step before a number goes into a leadership-facing report.
questions.professionalAnswer: I was doing my usual pre-send check on a monthly revenue dashboard before it went out, comparing the total against the prior month's trend, and the number was up about 40% with nothing in the business that explained a jump that size. I dug into it and found that a recent change to the order-line fact table's join logic had introduced a fan-out -- orders with multiple line items were getting double-counted on the revenue aggregate after a model change a few days earlier. Before fixing anything, I flagged it immediately to my manager and the stakeholder who was going to present it, explained specifically what was wrong and what the corrected number actually was, and held off sending the dashboard until the fix was verified rather than trying to quietly patch it in the background. Afterward, I added a row-count and total-revenue sanity check that runs automatically after that model refreshes and alerts if either number moves more than a reasonable threshold from the prior period, specifically so this exact category of silent fan-out issue gets caught by the pipeline itself next time, not by someone manually eyeballing a dashboard the night before a meeting.
commonMistakes: Giving a vague answer with no specific detection method or root cause
Describing quietly fixing the issue without proactively communicating it to the people who were about to use the number
Taking credit for 'catching' something that was actually caught by an automated alert with no personal judgment involved
Not describing any follow-up change made to prevent the same category of issue recurring
keyPoints: Describes a specific, credible detection method
Explains the actual root cause investigation
Proactively communicated the issue and the corrected number before anyone acted on bad data
Describes a concrete preventive change made afterward

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a specific, credible detection method
Explains a clear root cause investigation
Shows proactive, transparent communication of the issue
Describes a concrete preventive follow-up

questions.title: Balancing an Urgent Report Request Against a Pipeline Deadline
questions.prompt: You're in the middle of a tight deadline to migrate a critical ADF pipeline to a new source system, and a VP asks for an ad hoc Power BI report by end of day for an external meeting. Walk me through how you'd handle the conflict.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer doesn't default to either extreme -- dropping the migration entirely or refusing the VP outright -- and instead describes a quick, honest assessment of both the ad hoc request's real scope and the migration's actual slack or risk if delayed by a few hours. The candidate should describe clarifying the ad hoc request's true requirements first (does the VP need a polished new report, or would an existing report with a filter applied actually answer the question, which could take 20 minutes instead of several hours), since ad hoc requests are often overestimated in scope before being scoped properly. The answer should also show transparent communication upward -- telling the VP (or the VP's manager/the requester's chain) honestly about the competing deadline and either negotiating a slightly later delivery time, delivering a smaller-scope version that still answers the immediate need, or getting explicit sign-off that the migration deadline will slip, rather than silently doing both at reduced quality or silently deciding one doesn't matter without telling anyone. A strong answer closes with the actual outcome and reflects on what made that prioritization call defensible.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move is always to actually scope the new request before assuming it blows up my day -- a lot of 'I need a report by end of day' requests turn out to be answerable with an existing dashboard and a filter change in twenty minutes, not a from-scratch build. In this case, I'd ask the VP directly what decision the report needs to support for the external meeting, because that usually reveals whether I need the full new build or just a quick export of something that already exists. If it genuinely needs real work, I wouldn't just silently drop the migration or silently blow off the VP -- I'd go to whoever owns the migration deadline, usually my manager, and lay out the actual conflict honestly: here's the ask, here's the time it'll take, here's what slips if I take it on right now. Most of the time that conversation ends with either a short, explicit delay on the migration that everyone agreed to, or the VP getting a smaller-scope answer that still covers what they actually needed for the meeting. What I try to avoid is making that tradeoff decision silently on my own and letting someone find out later that one deadline moved without ever having agreed to it.
commonMistakes: Describing dropping the migration deadline silently without telling anyone it would slip
Describing refusing the VP's request outright without first trying to scope what they actually need
Not describing any upward communication about the competing priorities at all
Trying to do both at full scope simultaneously and describing it as a success without acknowledging the real tradeoff made
keyPoints: Scopes the new request's actual requirement before assuming the worst-case effort
Communicates the competing deadlines honestly rather than silently choosing one
Negotiates a concrete resolution (delay, reduced scope, or explicit sign-off) rather than guessing
Reflects on why the final prioritization call was defensible

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Shows scoping the new request before reacting
Shows transparent upward communication about the conflict
Describes a concrete, negotiated resolution
Reflects meaningfully on the decision

questions.title: Mentoring a Junior Analyst Through a Difficult DAX Problem
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you mentored a junior analyst or developer who was stuck on something technical, like a confusing DAX measure or a T-SQL query. What was your approach, and how did you know it actually helped them learn rather than just fixing it for them?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer describes a specific technical struggle a junior teammate had (a context-transition problem in DAX, a SARGability issue in a T-SQL query, a dbt incremental model double-counting) and emphasizes a teaching approach over simply handing over the fixed code -- asking guiding questions, walking through the underlying concept with a simpler example first, and having the junior person arrive at or at least actively participate in the fix rather than passively receiving it. The answer should include a concrete signal that the learning stuck, not just that the immediate problem was solved -- the junior person independently applying the same concept correctly on a later, different problem, explaining the concept back correctly to someone else, or catching a similar mistake themselves before it shipped. A strong answer also shows self-awareness about the tradeoff of mentoring time against an immediate deadline, acknowledging that teaching took longer in the moment than just fixing it directly would have, and explaining why that investment was worth it anyway.
questions.professionalAnswer: A junior analyst on my team was stuck on a DAX measure that kept returning the wrong number, and the root issue was a context transition problem -- she was trying to reference a measure inside a calculated column and getting unexpected results, but didn't yet have the mental model for why. Instead of just rewriting the formula for her, I pulled up a much simpler example first -- a one-row-at-a-time walkthrough of what row context versus filter context actually means -- and had her predict what a couple of small test formulas would return before running them, so she could see where her mental model and the actual behavior diverged. Once that clicked, I had her apply it back to her original measure herself rather than me just fixing it, which took noticeably longer than if I'd just handed her the corrected formula. The part that told me it actually landed was a few weeks later, when she caught a similar context transition issue in a teammate's measure during a review, before it ever got published, and explained the concept correctly to that teammate without needing me involved at all. That's the outcome I was actually going for -- not just the one measure getting fixed, but her being able to recognize and explain the pattern independently going forward.
commonMistakes: Describing simply fixing the problem directly without any real teaching component
Giving a vague answer with no specific technical concept or concrete follow-up evidence of learning
Not acknowledging the time tradeoff of mentoring versus just fixing it quickly
Describing the mentee's growth in generic terms with no specific, observable example of it sticking
keyPoints: Describes a specific technical concept the junior person was struggling with
Shows a genuine teaching approach, not just handing over the fixed solution
Provides concrete evidence the learning stuck beyond the immediate problem
Acknowledges the time tradeoff of mentoring and why it was worth it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a specific technical struggle and teaching approach
Provides concrete evidence the learning actually transferred
Acknowledges the mentoring time tradeoff thoughtfully

questions.title: Handling Two Stakeholders With Conflicting Requirements
questions.prompt: Describe a situation where two stakeholders wanted the same dashboard or dataset to behave in genuinely conflicting ways. How did you reach a resolution both could accept?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer names a specific, realistic conflict -- for example, a sales team wanting a pipeline dashboard to show deals at their most optimistic stage/value, while finance wants the same dashboard to show a more conservative, risk-adjusted view for forecasting, and both see the other's preferred version as 'wrong' for their purposes. The candidate should describe going beneath each stakeholder's stated request to understand the actual underlying need driving it, rather than treating the conflict as a simple compromise negotiation on the surface-level ask. A strong resolution usually isn't splitting the difference with a single, muddled middle-ground view that satisfies neither side well, but rather recognizing that both needs are legitimate and building a solution that serves both without compromising either -- a toggle/parameter letting the viewer switch between an optimistic and risk-adjusted view, or two clearly labeled, separate measures living in the same model so each team can build off the one relevant to them. The answer should close with confirmation that both stakeholders actually accepted and used the resulting solution, not just that a technical compromise was shipped.
questions.professionalAnswer: This happened with a sales pipeline dashboard -- sales wanted deal values shown at full potential value to stay motivated and track upside, while finance wanted the same dashboard risk-adjusted by stage-based close probability for their forecasting process, and each side thought the other's version was misleading for what they needed it for. Rather than trying to negotiate a single middle-ground number that would have satisfied neither side particularly well, I dug into why each team actually needed their version -- sales needed to see raw pipeline value to manage rep behavior day to day, finance needed a probability-weighted number to actually forecast revenue responsibly. Once I understood both needs were legitimate rather than one side just being wrong, I built both measures into the same model -- Pipeline Value (Full) and Pipeline Value (Weighted) -- clearly labeled, with a toggle on the dashboard letting either team switch to the view relevant to them, instead of forcing one default that one side would've had to live with. Both teams ended up actually adopting the dashboard regularly afterward, which told me the resolution actually worked, not just that I'd shipped something technically correct that nobody really used.
commonMistakes: Describing a surface-level compromise that satisfies neither stakeholder's actual underlying need
Not investigating the real reason behind each stakeholder's conflicting request before proposing a fix
Picking one stakeholder's side unilaterally without involving the other in the resolution
Ending the answer without confirming both stakeholders actually accepted and used the final solution
keyPoints: Describes a specific, realistic stakeholder conflict
Investigates the underlying need behind each stated request, not just the surface ask
Proposes a solution serving both needs rather than a muddled compromise
Confirms the resolution was actually accepted and used by both sides

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a specific, credible conflicting-requirements scenario
Shows investigation of the underlying need behind each request
Proposes a solution serving both needs rather than a weak compromise
Confirms real adoption/acceptance by both stakeholders

questions.title: Explaining a Technical Tradeoff to a Non-Technical Stakeholder
questions.prompt: Describe a time you had to explain a technical tradeoff, like DirectQuery versus Import, or why a dbt model couldn't just refresh instantly, to a non-technical stakeholder who needed to make a decision based on your explanation. How did you make it land?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer names a specific real tradeoff (DirectQuery's live-but-slower behavior versus Import's fast-but-stale behavior, or why a large incremental dbt model refresh takes a predictable amount of time rather than being instant) and describes translating it into terms the stakeholder's decision actually depended on, rather than explaining the underlying technology in technical depth for its own sake. The candidate should emphasize framing the explanation around the actual business consequence of each option -- 'this version is always current but every click will feel noticeably slower' versus 'this version is instant but only as current as this morning's refresh' -- using a concrete analogy or example relevant to the stakeholder's world rather than jargon. A strong answer also shows the stakeholder actually making an informed choice as a result, not just nodding along, and ideally describes checking understanding by having the stakeholder restate the tradeoff back in their own words before finalizing the decision.
questions.professionalAnswer: A marketing director needed to decide whether a campaign performance dashboard should connect live to our ad platform's data or run on a nightly refresh, and she didn't have the context to evaluate DirectQuery versus Import as technical terms, so I didn't lead with those terms at all. I framed it around what she'd actually experience: 'live' means every time you click into a different campaign, you're waiting a few extra seconds for fresh numbers, but those numbers are always current to the minute; 'nightly' means the dashboard feels instant to use, but the numbers you're looking at are as of this morning, not this exact moment. I tied that directly to her actual use case -- she mostly reviewed dashboards in the morning anyway, so a nightly refresh would feel just as current to her in practice as live would, while being noticeably faster to click through. I had her repeat the tradeoff back in her own words before we finalized it, which confirmed she really understood the choice rather than just agreeing because I'd recommended something -- she ended up choosing nightly, which was the right call for how she actually used the dashboard, and that's the outcome that told me the explanation had actually landed.
commonMistakes: Explaining the underlying technology in technical depth instead of translating it to a business consequence
Not tying the explanation to the stakeholder's specific decision or use case
Describing the stakeholder passively agreeing rather than confirming genuine understanding
Picking the answer for the stakeholder instead of equipping them to make an informed decision themselves
keyPoints: Names a specific, real technical tradeoff
Translates the tradeoff into business consequences, not technical jargon
Ties the explanation to the stakeholder's specific decision or use case
Confirms genuine understanding before the decision is finalized

questions.title: Pushing Back on a Rushed Migration Deadline
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you believed a deadline for a migration (such as a Snowflake or dbt cutover) was unrealistic or risky, and you had to push back. How did you make the case, and what happened?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer describes a specific migration scenario (a Snowflake cutover, a dbt project restructure, an ADF pipeline rewrite) and the concrete reason the deadline was risky -- not enough time for proper validation against the legacy system's output, a parallel-run period being cut short, or insufficient testing of a specific edge case (like a known data quality issue in the source that hadn't been fully scoped yet). The candidate should describe making the case with concrete evidence rather than a vague feeling -- a specific list of what validation steps would be skipped, or a quantified estimate of what going live without them actually risks (a specific report being wrong for a specific audience, a specific reconciliation that hasn't been run yet). A strong answer shows a constructive framing: not just raising the risk, but proposing a specific alternative, like a reduced scope for the original deadline with the riskier piece following shortly after, or a short, clearly-bounded extension with a concrete list of what that extra time buys. The answer should state the actual outcome honestly, including if leadership still decided to proceed on the original timeline, and how the candidate handled that outcome professionally.
questions.professionalAnswer: I was leading validation on a Snowflake cutover where the original migration deadline only left two days for comparing the new warehouse's output against the legacy system, and I didn't think that was enough time to properly reconcile a few known tricky areas, particularly a currency conversion step that had historically been a source of subtle bugs. I didn't just say 'this feels risky' -- I went to the project lead with a specific list: here are the five reconciliation checks that still need to run, here's roughly how long each takes, and here's specifically what could go wrong in production if we cut it to two days, using the currency conversion history as a concrete example of why that particular area deserved extra scrutiny. I proposed cutting over the lower-risk tables on the original date and holding the currency-sensitive tables for a few extra days until reconciliation was actually complete, rather than asking for a blanket delay on everything. Leadership agreed to the split approach, and when we did get to the currency tables a few days later, the extra reconciliation time actually caught a real rounding discrepancy that would have shipped wrong numbers if we'd pushed everything on the original deadline.
commonMistakes: Describing a vague worry about a deadline without concrete evidence or specifics
Raising the risk without proposing any specific alternative or path forward
Describing simply overriding the deadline unilaterally rather than making the case to the people who owned it
Giving an unrealistically tidy answer where everything goes exactly as proposed with no honest account of pushback or compromise
keyPoints: Describes a specific migration and a concrete, evidence-based reason for concern
Makes the case with specifics, not a vague feeling
Proposes a constructive alternative rather than just raising a risk
States the actual outcome honestly, including any compromise reached

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a specific migration scenario and concrete risk
Shows evidence-based, specific case-making rather than a vague concern
Proposes a constructive alternative
States an honest, credible outcome

questions.title: Responding to Critical Feedback on a Data Model's Design
questions.prompt: Describe a time a senior colleague or architect gave you critical feedback on a data model or pipeline design you were proud of. How did you respond in the moment, and did it change how you approached design afterward?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer describes a specific, substantive piece of feedback (a star schema design that didn't account for a role-playing dimension correctly, a dbt project structure that mixed staging and business logic in a way that would be hard to maintain, a fact table grain decision that would need to be redone once a new reporting requirement arrived) rather than a vague 'someone said my code was messy.' The candidate should be honest about their initial reaction -- some defensiveness or disappointment is normal and more credible than claiming instant total agreement -- but should then describe actually engaging with the substance of the critique rather than dismissing it, asking clarifying questions to fully understand the concern before responding. A strong answer shows a concrete change made as a result, either to that specific project or to the candidate's general approach going forward (a new habit of running a design past a senior colleague before building, a specific modeling principle they now apply by default), demonstrating the feedback genuinely changed behavior rather than just being accepted politely in the moment.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd built a dimensional model for a new reporting area and was genuinely proud of how clean the fact table looked, and a senior architect pointed out that I'd picked the wrong grain -- I'd modeled at the order level when a reporting requirement that was already on the roadmap would need line-item-level detail, which meant the model would need to be rebuilt within a few months anyway. My honest first reaction was some defensiveness, because I'd put real thought into the design and the feedback meant redoing meaningful work. But I asked him to walk me through specifically why line-item grain mattered for that upcoming requirement, rather than just accepting or rejecting the feedback on the spot, and once I actually understood the reasoning, it was clearly right -- I'd optimized for what was easy to build today instead of what the business was actually going to need soon. I rebuilt the model at the correct grain, and more importantly, I changed my actual process going forward -- I now explicitly ask about the roadmap of known upcoming requirements before finalizing a fact table's grain, instead of just designing for the requirement directly in front of me, which is a habit that feedback gave me and has saved me from the same mistake more than once since.
commonMistakes: Giving a vague answer with no specific, substantive feedback described
Claiming instant, uncomplicated agreement with no honest acknowledgment of an initial reaction
Describing accepting the feedback politely but not actually changing any behavior or approach afterward
Framing the story as proving the feedback was wrong, rather than genuinely engaging with and learning from it
keyPoints: Describes specific, substantive critical feedback
Honestly acknowledges an initial reaction before describing genuine engagement
Shows asking clarifying questions to understand the critique before responding
Describes a concrete, lasting change in approach as a result

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes specific, substantive feedback
Shows honest, credible reaction and genuine engagement
Shows understanding-seeking before responding
Describes a concrete, lasting behavior change

questions.title: Catching and Disclosing Your Own Production Mistake
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you caught a mistake you personally made in a production pipeline or report, after it had already gone live. How did you handle disclosing it and fixing it?
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer describes a specific, real mistake (an incremental model's filter boundary that missed late-arriving rows, a MERGE condition matching on the wrong key and silently overwriting unrelated rows, a DAX measure deployed with an ALL instead of an ALLSELECTED that quietly inflated a percentage for a few days) owned clearly and without excessive hedging or blame-shifting onto a reviewer, a tool, or unclear requirements. The candidate should describe disclosing the mistake proactively and promptly to whoever was affected, rather than quietly fixing it and hoping no one noticed the gap or the earlier wrong numbers, including being specific about what was wrong, for how long, and what the impact actually was, so affected stakeholders can judge for themselves whether any decisions need to be revisited. The answer should describe the actual fix and any immediate mitigation taken, and close with a concrete process change made afterward specifically to prevent a repeat of that category of mistake, showing the incident led to a durable improvement rather than just an apology.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd deployed a MERGE statement for a customer dimension upsert, and a few days later I noticed some customer addresses looked wrong during an unrelated investigation -- it turned out my MERGE condition had matched on a column that wasn't actually unique in a small subset of cases, and it had silently overwritten the wrong customer's address with another customer's data for about forty records over three days. I didn't quietly patch it and move on -- I immediately told my manager and the team that used that dimension table what had happened, specifically which customers were affected, how long the bad data had been live, and what I believed the impact was, so they could decide for themselves whether anything downstream needed to be reviewed or corrected, not just take my word that it was fine now. I fixed the MERGE condition to match on the actual unique key and reran a full reconciliation to identify and correct every affected row, not just the ones I happened to notice. Afterward, I added a pre-deployment check specifically for any new MERGE statement that verifies the match condition is backed by an actual unique constraint before it ships, because the root cause wasn't bad luck, it was a gap in my own review process that I wanted closed for good, not just fixed this one time.
commonMistakes: Describing quietly fixing the mistake without proactively disclosing it to affected stakeholders
Shifting blame onto a reviewer, a tool, or unclear requirements instead of owning the mistake directly
Giving a vague answer with no specific technical mistake or concrete impact described
Not describing any process change made afterward to prevent the same category of mistake recurring
keyPoints: Describes a specific, real technical mistake, owned clearly without blame-shifting
Discloses the mistake proactively and specifically to affected stakeholders
Describes a thorough fix, including reconciling the full scope of impact, not just the first symptom noticed
Describes a concrete, durable process change made to prevent recurrence

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Describes a specific mistake, owned clearly and honestly
Shows proactive, specific disclosure to affected stakeholders
Describes a thorough fix addressing full impact scope
Describes a concrete preventive process change
